Seventeenth coarse span: pages 6 to 21 open in the missing-value subsection 3.2, then carry section 4 on the three-dimensional vector assessment model with its twelve indices, its three normalisation formulas and its GDM-EWM weighting, section 5 on the curved-surface target model with the two elasticity indicators and the vision for India, section 6 on the policies for three terms and the timeline, and section 7 on the N-Verhulst forecast, the validity assessment and the impact analysis, so one span holds five numbered sections and the whole forecast half of the paper. The naming habit is the sentence-opener kind in its most extreme form: 222 names for 5,817 words, many of them fragments with the numbers and nouns deleted, so the list carries "will be better when" four times, "is calculated as" three times, "is shown as follows" twice and "where respectively" twice. Five names cannot be located and are `unresolved` because they are single words with many equally good referents - "shows" eleven times in the span, "while" five times, "reflects" twice on the EDE and the Gini sentences, "is" a hundred and twenty-three times, and "but and" not at all after the line wraps; "considers" resolves because it occurs once, on FSI, and the two "adjusts" resolve because the Em sentence and the Etheta sentence are the only two. The model is a vector rather than a scalar: SD, ST and SI each scored by their weighted indices, S0 = (1,1,1) as the ideal, |S| read as the current level and the deviation angle theta read as the balance, so the diagnostic language is modulus and angle rather than a grade. That is why the target is a curved surface, radius r = Em(sqrt(3) - x) + x and half-angle phi = Etheta times theta, with HDI, FSI and Gini as the three non-educational elasticity indicators; for India r = 1.22 and phi = 11.5 degrees against a current |S| = 0.735 and theta = 23.13 degrees. The validity test then forecasts the three components without intervention by N-Verhulst and reports 2040 at S = (0.58, 0.61, 0.50) with the angle under 11.5 degrees.

note: Read pages 6-22 (37,920 characters) end to end. Eighteenth coarse span in the harmless direction: pages 6 to 22 open on Figure 2, one line above the section 6 heading, and carry the whole Theil model (6.1 to 6.3.4), the oligopoly and Shapley chapters 7.1 to 7.5, the path-analysis and scenario chapter 8.1 to 8.2.3, and the opening of chapter 9, so the span holds three numbered chapters and never touches the paper's policy half. Naming is the descriptive family again, 135 names for 4,258 words and 152 sentences, so nearly one name per sentence, and all 135 resolve. What the paper does is worth recording because it is a different move from the index builders: it takes a published inequality index and re-points its object. Equity is quoted from the New Palgrave as the absence of envy, and the Theil index is then extended from persons to countries by replacing income with composite national power, with the naive extension rejected by a counterexample (the United States and the Vatican would have to be power-equal) and repaired twice - a population-size weight, then a logarithmic transformation - so three derive blocks carry the whole model. Comprehensive power is then a factor analysis over twelve variables, residuals dropped on the strength of the correlations, m = 3 factors passing eighty percent, and the composite score substituted for income. The rest of the chapter is scenario arithmetic on one index: four grade sets, a mineral named Lucky that lifts a mining country's GDP by 15%, a second mineral Lucky2 that makes the payout rule explicit, a third Lucky3 that lifts every indicator by 0.05, and the same Theil plot redrawn after each: within-group curves fluctuate, the capable-versus-incapable curve jumps, and a Shapley allocation at 0.6437 and 0.5982 makes every curve fall. That is why define is thirty-two, interpret twenty-eight and read-figure twelve - the paper builds one index and then reads it back five times.

Twentieth coarse span, and it is wrong at the top end: pages 6 to 21 open inside the assumptions list, on Assumption 2 and its justification, so the first four assumptions of the paper sit above the span and only Assumptions 2 to 5 are inside it; the span then carries section 3 Model I (the capability approach, individual welfare, the three factors, the twenty-five indicators, EWM weights, GDI and the peace index, and the coefficient-of-variation equity measure with its validation), all of section 4 Model II (the GE matrix, the three asteroid types, cost, mass, time, NPV, the ME-MI investment model, the Cournot oligopoly and the 2011UW-158 example), all of section 5 on how the model changes when the throughput factor or the number of mining countries changes, and the first lines of section 6 on policy - so one span holds three numbered chapters, one of them a second model, plus the opening of the policy chapter. Naming is the descriptive family, 117 names for 4,303 words and 257 sentences, so one name per two sentences, and all 117 resolve; one of them records a printed figure-number error without losing its block, "splits countries into those needing investment and those funding themselves", which the paper attributes to Figure 6 but prints in the Figure 10 discussion. What the chapter is worth recording for is the equity measure: this is the only model in the sample that measures inequity with a coefficient of variation rather than a ratio or a distance. Each country gets an asset index and an achievement index from the same EWM pipeline, EI is their synthesis, and global equity is CV = sigma/mean over all countries, so every result in the paper is one number moving - 1.2437 and 0.5766 in 2000, 1.5332 and 0.6912 in 2020, 1.5379 and 0.6945 after one mining operation, 1.5383 and 0.6946 when the throughput factor quadruples, 1.5359 when the third level of countries joins - and the verdict is always the same sentence shape, the coefficient rose so the gap widened. That is why define is thirty-five blocks, compute fourteen and mechanism thirteen, with interpret only twelve, and why the sensitivity chapter is arithmetic on the same two numbers rather than a re-derivation.

note: Read pages 7-21 (36,110 characters) end to end. Twenty-first coarse span: pages 7 to 21 open on Table 2, the data sources, and 2.3.2 Data Filling, so the span begins one subsection above the model chapter; it then carries all of section 3 (the D&E model: four requirements, twelve inferior indicators in three dimensions, the two-layer EWM and coefficient-of-variation weighting, the Mahalanobis-distance equity score), all of section 4 (who mines, the AMO redistribution design and the P&A model), all of section 5 (the fund-pool and participation variants) and the opening of section 6 on policy - four numbered sections, and the names put no block on the data-filling bullets that open it. Naming is the descriptive family, 92 names for 4,329 words and 214 sentences, so one name per two and a half sentences, and all 92 resolve. Two things are worth copying. The first is the two-layer weighting: EWM weights the twelve inferior indicators inside each dimension and a coefficient-of-variation weighting sets the three dimension weights, so the index is built twice with no judgement asked at either level. The second is that equity is read as a distance, not a ratio: each country is a point (EMDI, TDI, EGDI), the Mahalanobis distance to the centre is summarised in a score with a mean, a maximum and a spread term, and GEI = 1000 over that score, so the paper can report 66.80 before mining and 74.67 after fifty years and speak of a 27-year recovery. Its weakness is visible in the same construction: the redistribution is the model's own invention, so the result that mining raises equity in the long run is a result about the AMO design rather than about asteroid mining, and the paper says so only indirectly when it tests the fund-pool size in section 5.1.

Four subsections pass with no block at all - 3.1.1 to 3.1.4 define social, energy, technology and economic equity in one paragraph each and none is named; 3.3 Data Preprocessing names neither the three missing-value methods nor the cost-benefit-moderate normalisation; and the entropy, coefficient-of-variation, K-means, comparative-advantage and grey-model derivations carry no name between them, because each is introduced by a name at the top of its subsection (4, 5, 7, 12) and then runs to the formula. So the two F extremes are one design decision seen twice: how finely the paper cuts its paragraphs, and whether a formula paragraph earns a block of its own. Four route blocks open sections rather than sentences (5, 10, 12, 17), which is the chapter's dominant habit; the two source blocks are the only citations the chapter makes in its own voice (2, 7), and the TOPSIS block names its authors and decade and nothing else. The equity argument is thin where it matters: fifteen of the twenty-one blocks are define, interpret, route or source, and the whole model chapter contains one compute block, one compare block, one select block and one read-figure block.

note: Read pages 5-19 (56,321 characters) end to end. Twenty-third coarse span: it opens at the 3 Model Preparation heading, so the notation table and the data-collection and data-filling pages sit above the model, and it closes inside 7.2.2, so sections 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 - the preparation, the equity model, the asteroid partial equilibrium, the impact chapter and the optimisation landscape - all count as one model chapter, five numbered sections in fifteen pages. The naming is the sixth habit and the one no reader would guess: every name is the sentence's grammatical skeleton with its content left as a placeholder - "we-observe-when-same must-both-equal-1", "goodness-of-fit close-to-1 therefore-fitting-good", "we-calculate-T=N coefficient-become much-lower", "select-N-common-factors eigenvalue-greater" - so the list locates blocks exactly, nothing is unresolved, and it says what shape each sentence has rather than what the block does. That is why the coding has to be done from the page: the same skeleton can be a check (10, the limiting case where equal RE and OE force both to one), a compute block (18, T=50 giving GE=0.4521) or a select block (22, four eigenvalues above one), and the placeholders hide every number the paper actually prints - R-squared 0.8957, Rand index 0.85, Bartlett 234.01, cumulative contribution 62.545 percent, GE 0.4521. The chapter's real weakness under this taxonomy is that it derives nothing: there is not one derive block in five sections, although the pages print the benefit-cost-interval normalisation, the entropy chain, the four chain-growth ratios and the T dataset, the exponential smoothing of dataset 2, the y = x^a fit, the integral that defines GE, the Ward sum of squares and the Rand index, the factor loading matrix and the Cobb-Douglas production function. The chapter is coded instead as five checks, five routes, four definitions and three sources, which is what the names lead a coder to do: they open subsections and report fit statistics, and the algebra between the openings goes unlabelled.

Twenty-fourth coarse span and the first that opens inside an assumption bullet and closes inside the policy chapter: page 5 begins mid-bullet, so the scarcity premise and the four assumptions above it carry no block, and the span then carries section 4 on the HELEN index, section 5 on the asteroid market, section 6 on the model adjustment and the opening of section 7 on royalties - four numbered sections, and the policy paragraph that closes the span carries no block at all. Naming is the template family again, 20 names for roughly 5,800 words with content in placeholders, so the list locates blocks and hides every number: the HELEN index rises from 0.525 to 0.579, market shares come out 53.20, 26.13, 15.22, 5.16 and 0.0 percent, GDP change 1.54, 0.68, 0.04, 0.01 and 0.00 percent, and the two names in the validation paragraph (6, 7) are the several-names-in-one-paragraph defect, since the whole verification is two sentences. Two things are worth taking. The first is the regulator as a constraint: the Moon Agreement's due regard becomes a market-share cap 0 <= q_i <= delta_i^U Q inside the Cournot programme, so section 5 needs no separate policy argument, and section 6.2 then re-solves without the cap and compares - the restricted peak is 0.789 against 0.739 unrestricted, the inflection comes at 1800 firms against 1200 - so the policy is tested as a model variant rather than recommended. The second is the sign convention printed once in a parenthesis before the result table, 'the larger the value of the global equity index, the worse the equity', which is the only place the reader is told which way the index runs. The chapter derives ten equations - AHP weighting, the entropy chain, the factor model, Cobb-Douglas, the cost function, the Cournot programme, three GDP and DI and PPI change rates - and the names mark none of them, so its four compute blocks are the two results it most wants read (12, 15) and its check blocks are the two sentences of its one validation.

Twenty-sixth coarse span: it opens inside the assumption list, one sentence into a bullet on technology diffusion, so the glossary and the assumptions carry no block above it, and it closes inside 6.3 on policy recommendations, so sections 3 to 6 - the GGDP accounting, the fuzzy climate evaluation, the spatial game and the time-dimension carrying capacity, and the Australia case with its PVAR - pass as one model chapter, and the policy bullets at the foot belong to no block. This is the only chapter in the ledger whose names include a section title: block 6 is "It's time to make the right choice", which is the heading of task 3 printed as a name, so a name here marks a task boundary rather than a paragraph. The first is the conversion of a policy into a growth-rate adjustment: the GGDP standard is assumed to cut the growth of Eco2, Waste and NRR by a policy factor theta = 3%, that 3% is calibrated off two events (the 2007-2008 crisis and the 2014 Sino-US statement), and every later result inherits it, so the chapter's whole forecast rests on one number that appears in a sentence and not in an equation. note: Read pages 6-20 (43,596 characters of body, 5,645 words, 197 sentences) end to end. Twenty-seventh coarse span, and the first in a while whose opening is clean: it starts on the section 4 heading itself, so nothing above is orphaned. It is the tail that is cut - the span stops mid-sentence in 7.3, on "On the other hand, the economic situation of Brunei itself is", so the exhaustion arithmetic is named and its consequence, the collapse the paper goes on to model, belongs to no block. Twenty names for 5,645 words is one name per 282 words, which puts this paper beside P-F-2022-2218577 at the sparse end of the range rather than beside the sentence-list papers. What the names attach to is the rhetorical turn, not the model: three of the twenty are colon-labels ("three-category survey:", "EWM weight rationale:", "costs-discussion headed:") and seven are the paper's own sentence openers printed as names ("from-figures-observe", "seems-to-indicate", "it-can-be-foreseen", "no-one-knows then we-all-know", "it-is-worth-noting", "of-course-different", "in-any-case fortunately"), the third of the six naming habits, at its purest here. One name is a new kind and worth recording as a seventh habit: block 11 is "a bold topic heading (Intergenerational Equity), then a paragraph that unpacks the dilemma", a typesetting instruction rather than a sentence, so it names the shape of the page and none of the paper's words can be recovered from it. The cost of this naming is visible: the 21-indicator table, the four normalisation formulas, the three EWM steps, Table 3's five regressions, the GGDP rewrite and the ARIMA / GM(1,1) / SVM comparison all pass unnamed, so the chapter's whole computation chain has no name on it, and the coded mix has no derive block at all although the chapter prints a dozen formulas. Three moves are worth keeping. The first is a single scalar carrying the paper: percentDIF = |GDP - GGDP| / GDP is defined once at 4.3, and the same number then appears in the Table 3 regressions, in the ln(-%DIF) trend, in the forecast equations and in the climate rescoring, so one ratio holds the three sections together. The second is naming the payback year: the year the reformed curve overtakes the unreformed one is called the Intersection, it is forecast per country from the resource dependence rate, and Figure 10 reports it per country instead of reporting one world number, which turns a global claim into a map. The third is the three-forecaster arbitration: ARIMA and GM(1,1) are run, ARIMA is rejected because it turns the score negative in 2038 and GM(1,1) because it runs negative in 2080, SVM because it is flat, and the range is then fixed by logistic normalisation with x0 set to the median - a check that rejects models for being implausible rather than for fitting badly, and the case study is chosen the same way, Brunei because it is the extreme (60% of GDP and 90% of exports from oil and gas, GGDP per capita outside the top 100) rather than because it is typical. Section headings alliterate on M - Method, Model, Mould, Movement - which is an F-level surface trick, cheap to copy and visible on every page.

note: Read pages 5-19 (38,022 characters of body, 5,208 words, 178 sentences) end to end. Twenty-eighth coarse span and wrong at both ends again: it opens on the notation table of section 3, so the symbol list and the data description of section 4 - the six databases, the World Bank and OECD links - carry no block at all, and it closes mid-sentence in 8.3, inside the description of the EPS model, so the policy simulation the paper was building toward is never named. Eighteen names for 5,208 words is one name per 289 words, sparser still than P-F-2023-2311517 at 282 and P-F-2022-2218577 at 262. The naming family is the third habit with a label glued on: every name is a hyphenated key, a colon, and then the paper's own first clause - "two-perspectives survey:", "more-established choice:", "no-perfect-standard then simpler:", "figure-three-conclusions:" - so the list is readable at a glance and still tells the coder nothing about the job, which had to be taken from the page in every one of the eighteen cases. Three moves are worth taking. The first is the mediator: a single Climate Index is inserted between the economy and the climate, CI is regressed on GGDP with R-squared 0.987, the policy is simulated by substituting GGDP for GDP from 2000, and the finding is the difference between the two delta-CI paths read as a scalar phi - 31.57% slower deterioration on average, 5.23% during the subprime and COVID years - so a qualitative question ('does the measure help') is answered by one number with a stated sign convention and one honest exception. The second is monetising that index, which is the step that makes the cost-benefit chapter possible at all: PU in dollars is the same delta-CI difference divided by the regression slope and shifted by the intercept, so any non-monetary index in a paper can be priced by the coefficient that links it to money, and the downside is PD = delta-GDP minus delta-GDP-prime plus a correction term. The third is that correction term, and it is the most inventive and the weakest link at once: multilateral resistance is borrowed from gravity-trade work, the paper clusters 178 countries by GGDP per capita against the rate of climate deterioration, reads the four colour groups as four attitudes (green endorses, orange accepts, red resists, blue follows), and then prices resistance as Pt = k * sum of the distances the red countries must travel out of the red region, with k and b never estimated - so 'the upside is smaller than the downside for almost every year' is a sign, not a magnitude, and the chapter's verdict rests on an unexplained constant. Two smaller things to copy: the sector ratio ECRi = ECi / (NRDC + EDC) turns the national accounting identity into a per-sector share, which is how the paper gets to four sectors carrying 89.2% of environmental cost, and the ten-year plan prints three dated targets (18% off CO2 intensity by 2030, green manufacturing output, 72% off carbon intensity by 2050) that give the policy chapter something checkable. One slip is worth recording because it decides a block: the cluster discussion says 'as shown in Figure 7' but the cluster figure is Figure 8, and the ten-year target printed as 11 trillion RMB in the text is printed as $11 trillion in the schedule figure.

note: Read pages 7-18 (27,885 characters of body, 3,166 words, 117 sentences) end to end. Twenty-ninth coarse span, clean at the top and cut at the tail: it starts on the section 3 heading (Task1) and stops after Figure 12 in 6.2, so the impact section's own conclusion carries no block. Fifteen names for 3,166 words is one per 211 words, the densest of the last four but still a task-level rather than paragraph-level list: one name per task section, or two. The naming family is the 2315018 habit again - a hyphenated key, a colon, then the paper's own clause - with the content replaced by bracketed placeholders ("[N] former projects", "[area] draws large amounts", "[client] from two aspects"), so it is the template family and the label family at once and nothing in it can be turned into a job without the page. The page is a grant proposal rather than a model chapter, and that is what is worth keeping: four task sections answer four questions with documents, not with equations - 3.1 maps 764 former projects and names SEA the trending area, 3.2 draws the IWT value chain, runs results-based management and the logic framework into a problem tree, an objective tree, a logframe matrix and a Gantt chart, 4 ranks seven specialised IOs on a three-level indicator system and picks WWF at 78.70, and only then does the chapter produce algebra. Two devices from the ranking half are worth copying. The first is that the index does the choosing and the paper says so: scores from 15.81 to 78.70, the highest one executes the project, and the three indicator families are explained in one line each (organisational, communication, special influence) so the reader can see why WWF wins before seeing the number. The second is that the client is then argued to, not merely chosen: a UN Comtrade flow map establishes that SEA is the core, and a grey relational analysis over UNODC trafficking series establishes that tigers rank first at 0.83 against live reptiles 0.80 and pangolins 0.68, so the proposal's target is defended by two rankings of existing data - a cheap and honest substitute for a model that cannot be built. The one real model is the cooperation section: an expected utility with legal and illegal income, a penalty cost, a detection rate r, a Lagrange function and four comparative statics, from which 'raising r lowers the illegal share' is the whole result, and the argument that Interpol brings force while WWF brings expertise is what makes r rise. Its weakness is stated in the same place it is used: the sign of the comparative static is asserted from the signs of the derivatives (numerator negative, denominator positive) and the closed forms never appear. The impact model is OLS turned ridge: four explanatory variables and VIFs of 15.069, 13.08, 15.908 and 4.43, the switch to ridge, a trace that fixes the parameter at 0.022, and a final R-squared of 0.991 with F = 54.485 - all on n = 7 by year, which the paper reports and does not discuss, and which is the honest limit of a seven-year series with four regressors. One corpus fact has to be recorded because it decides how this chapter can be reused: the extraction has lost the algebra. All six EWM equations, the utility function, the FOCs and the ridge equations print as empty parentheses in the text, and the page also carries stray non-English watermark characters, so the names are the only reliable locator for the blocks and any clone has to take the formulas from the rendered page.

note: Read pages 6-21 (88,355 characters of body, 7,675 words, 278 sentences) end to end, the longest chapter read so far. Thirtieth coarse span, wrong at both ends: page 6 opens inside the data-completion bullet list that sits above the model chapter (kindred complement, fitting complement), so the missing-value machinery carries no block, and the span stops mid-sentence in 5.6, inside the sensitivity figures. Fourteen names for 7,675 words is one per 548 words, against 289 in the sparsest of the last three, so this list is pitched at the subsection rather than the paragraph and is the coarsest read in this run. The family is the 2024 habit seen in the last three papers: a hyphenated key, a colon, then the clause, with the numbers replaced by placeholders ("[vector]", "[N]%", "$[N] billion"), so again no name yields a job. What the page shows is worth taking because the chapter's spine is unusual. It evaluates clients on a triangle of power, resources and interests, weights six indicators per corner by EWM, draws each candidate as a radar triangle, and then ranks the three categories by AHP - enterprises 1.822, governments 1.646, NGOs 0.5022 - so the choice of an enterprise client is made by an index and confirmed by a second method. The genuinely novel device is in section 4: instead of choosing a single client, the paper computes the client's complement, the vector of what LVMH lacks (0.56, 0.06, 0.76), and then searches every other profiled client by cosine similarity for the one whose strengths point in exactly that direction, landing on the government of Seychelles at 99.9% with the vector (0.35, 0.03, 0.46). That is a partner-selection rule a reader can lift whole: define the gap, then match the gap rather than the client. The profit argument is the cheap second half of the same idea - Apple's iPhone revenue of 2.01e10 times the 4.7% leather share as the cost, the mean of three comparable R&D budgets at 4.310e9 as the investment, industry sales forecasts for the return, and then an affine mapping to LVMH at 128.06e9 - which is a proportional-scaling argument the paper names honestly as roughly proportional. Three things in the results half are worth recording against it. First, the regression runs five trade categories on eight years with R-squared 0.979 and VIFs from 4.65 to 14.175, and unlike the same year's 2409949 paper this one lists the collinearity and does nothing about it. Second, the one arithmetic check a reader can run fails: 25.6 billion falling to 17.54 billion is a 31.5% fall, and the paper prints 33.81%, so the sentence that claims the target was met does not follow from its own two numbers. Third, in the five-point estimation the deviation q is printed as 2 where (5 - 4) / 0.667 gives 1.5, and the 97.3% and 87.2% that follow are not reproducible from the formulas as printed. The block list is too coarse to have caught any of these, which is the cost of one name per subsection.

note: Read pages 7-20 (31,192 characters of body, 3,944 words, 136 sentences) end to end. Thirty-first coarse span, wrong at both ends again: page 7 opens on equations 7 to 9, the tail of the probability-matrix section that belongs above the model chapter, so the AHP and EWM algebra that precedes the first block carries no name, and the span stops mid-sentence in 9.1 just after the Poisson setup. Fifteen names for 3,944 words, one per 263 words, at the sparse end, in the same 2024 family - key, colon, clause, numbers replaced by placeholders. The device worth taking is the use of a canonical dynamic model as an evaluation instrument: poachers are the prey and the conservation organisation the predator, and the three Lotka-Volterra coefficients are then read as organisational capabilities - PUR is the predation rate (chance of encounter times enforcement efficiency), SR the conversion rate (public support times political support), PER the reciprocal of predator mortality (funding and attention). Once the coefficients are capabilities the paper can weight them by AHP (0.43, 0.35, 0.22), score candidates on them, and choose INO at 0.51 against GA 0.42 and PAP 0.37 through CAI = (1 + IN)(CI * SC), which is a way of making a capability argument arithmetic without inventing an index. The rest of the chapter is a chain of standard pieces wired to that choice: a BP network trained on 248 records for 736 iterations, a TSP over 166 countries solved by simulated annealing, a greedy selection of five monitoring countries at a 1,000 km radius, and a heat map that reports a 23.5% fall in trade. Two things in that chain are worth recording because a writer would repeat them. First, the TSP answer is 1,696 days for one global publicity cycle, which is four and a half years of a five-year plan spent travelling, and the paper reports the number without noticing what it does to the schedule. Second, the reporting defects are the kind that survive into a submitted paper: the four R values are printed as 0.997, 0.939, 0.929 and 0.923 with the fourth labelled training for the second time, the paragraph comparing PUR and SR across the three candidates is printed twice verbatim, and the impediment model puts a Poisson lambda of 30 on bad-weather days without saying what the 30 counts. The block list at fifteen names cannot see any of this, and the one name that does name a check - 'these four R values are very close to 1' - is the check that passes.

Two consequences follow and both are recordable. First, several names keep no content at all: 'it can be observed that the higher the [variable], the lower the [outcome]' is a template that would fit any paper in the corpus, and 'percentage-result table' names an artifact, not a sentence. Second, the first name is cut mid-word in storage ('net revenue from [lega') and the sentence it was taken from opens 'The conditions driving IWT behaviors were, in fact, when...', so the span opens one clause late. The span is also wrong at the top and at the tail: page 10 is the notation table and Figure 2, both unnamed, and the tail stops after the Table 2 reading, leaving the closing 'More importantly...' paragraph and section 6 unnamed - unlike the last five papers this one stops at a paragraph boundary rather than mid-sentence. The architectural device is worth taking whole: the chapter builds a micro model and then reuses it at macro level with one bridge sentence - after obtaining the micro-level model we have the ability to discuss the macro-level effects generated by the superposition of micro effects - and every qualitative goal is then forced into a normalised weighted sum, government goal as a1 GIWT + a2 GGDP + a3 Gequ with the weights summing to 1, GDP growth as wc dC + wi dI + wg dG with weights summing to 1, so the policy question becomes one scalar maximisation over one decision variable, the split between infrastructure and agricultural subsidy. Two smaller moves travel well. Distributive equity is measured as a ratio of the two wage changes rather than a level, so it needs no distributional data. And the budget constraint is anchored to last year's growth, Bt = Bt-1 + rho(dInfra + dSub), which makes the programme self-financing and turns rho into the actual ask. Against that, three things a reader can check do not hold. Eq 11 prints ti = max{0, -53 wi + 20}, so any hourly wage above 20/53 = 0.38 dollars drives the model answer to zero, which means the calibration predicts that nobody in Tanzania poaches, and the paper then justifies a sixteen-year eradication path with that model. The constants 53 and 20 appear nowhere with a substitution table, so the closed form cannot be reproduced from Table 1. And three horizons are used without ever being reconciled - sixteen years to eradicate, a thirty-year optimisation cycle, five years of short-term effects - each section choosing its own. Corpus defect to record: the Table 1 notation block is interleaved by the CHIP and MATHmodels watermarks so symbols, descriptions and values are misaligned row by row, and a clone must rebuild that table from the render.

Thirty-fourth F chapter and the first 2025 paper in the run, so the naming family changes completely: these names do not describe a block's content at all, they label a sentence pattern and quote its opener - 'Model selection justification chain: "The reason for choosing...is mainly based on" followed by enum', 'Advantage enumeration with transitions: "First...Secondly...In addition...Finally"', 'Summary sentence with conditional reasoning: "In summary, given the...it is reasonable to choose"', 'Finding-bullet pattern with "characterized by"'. That is the eighth naming habit, after fragments, the printing-error note, the sentence-opener, the descriptive list, the opening-only list, the placeholder template and the layout instruction, and it is the one that makes coding hardest, because a name of this kind can only be matched if the reader recognises the pattern in the pages. The names are also one per sentence rather than one per block: three consecutive names (selection chain, advantage enumeration, summary sentence) all describe the same justification paragraph for the variational Bayesian Gaussian mixture model, so a paragraph of 250 words carries three blocks. Extraction is the worst in the ledger so far and has to be recorded before anything else: 665 of the 2,208 tokens in the span, thirty per cent, are the m-runs left where Figures 4 and 5 were, so the prose the names describe is about 1,543 words and the density is one name per 193 words of real text rather than one per 276. The span is also wrong at both ends: page 7 opens at 5.2, so section 5.1 and whatever precedes it carry no name, and the tail stops inside the fourth finding bullet at 'This can greatly increase the possibility of bringing criminals to justice'. One layout defect inside the span is worth recording because it is the kind that survives review: Table 2, an EM algorithm for censored survival data, is printed in the middle of 5.2.2 between the VBGMM text and Figure 4, with no sentence anywhere referring to it, so a clustering section carries a survival-analysis table from another part of the paper. On what the chapter shows: the two-level structure is a clean template - level one regresses the outcome on case-level factors, level two regresses the level-one intercepts on country-level factors, and the paper writes both out as explicit equations, three log-odds equations for four outcome categories at layer one and three intercept equations on five Z indices borrowed from the GCI index at layer two - so the whole country-level story is carried by five numbers per outcome rather than a second model. Three checks a reader can run on it. The collinearity pre-check is asserted and not shown: the sentence says the variance inflation factor is below 10 'within a reasonable range' with no table and no values. No fit statistic appears anywhere in the span - no log-likelihood, no AIC, no sample size, no p values - so none of the twelve printed coefficients can be falsified. And the coefficients themselves are on a raw scale: -16.351 and 11.218 on log-odds are odds ratios of 1e-7 and 7e4, which means the predictors were never standardised and the layers are not comparable, while the finding bullets then read the signs in words: the success bullet says 'fewer assets exposed to potential attackers' although the X2 term in the success equation is the only positive one printed, so either X2 is coded as exposure rather than security or the prose reverses the sign, and the paper never says which.

note: Read pages 7-16 (40,247 characters of extraction, 3,814 tokens, 118 sentences) end to end. Thirty-fifth F chapter and the second 2025 paper, thirteen names for 3,814 tokens, one per 293, or one per 191 of the 2,485 real words once the 1,329 m-tokens are removed - thirty-five per cent of the span is figure noise left by the watermark. The naming family is a third kind in two papers: the 2025 habit is the imperative instruction. Every name here is a verb-first order to the writer with no subject and no content - 'Introduce selected algorithm with core principle', 'State objective function in plain language before formula', 'Reference prior claim to justify hyperparameter selection method', 'Transition from clustering results to next model by claiming factor identification', 'Motivate custom formulation by citing domain-specific structure' - so the list reads as annotation guidance about how a block should be built rather than as a description of what this block does. That is the closest the corpus comes to publishing its own rubric, and it is the easiest family to confuse with the layout-instruction habit, the difference being that those describe the page and these describe the rhetoric. The span is wrong at both ends: page 7 opens mid-sentence inside the one-hot encoding of section 4.1 ('method, each categorical feature mentioned above was converted into a binary vector'), so the preprocessing that the clustering depends on carries no name, and the tail stops inside the third of the high-GCI bullets on page 16. The equations are the real loss in this chapter and a clone has to know it: the K-means objective, both Gower distance formulas, the regularised objective with its Hadamard product, the Lagrange solution, the association strength matrix, the constraint and the integer programming model all come out of the extraction as parenthetical symbol glossaries with the formulas themselves missing, so only text survives and every equation must be taken from the render. On the chapter's argument, two structural moves and two defects. The move is the layering of a data-driven half on a theory half: K-means with elbow-chosen K, chi-square screening of features, PCA for display, then a mapping of every cluster onto a Chinese Five Elements scheme whose generation and restriction relations become the model's constraints, so a clustering result is re-read as five elements with an association matrix and a mutual generation/restriction matrix of 1 and -1. That is a strong template for a paper that needs a theory spine without inventing one: cluster first, then rename the clusters. The defects are both circularities of the same kind. The elbow chooses K = 5 and the model then has exactly five elements, one cluster per element, so the data cannot disagree with the theory; and the cluster summaries are printed as bare thresholds - firewall deployment above 70%, social network attacks above 50%, DDoS above 60% - which the next section reuses verbatim as the criteria that define Metal, Wood and Fire, so a centroid becomes a theoretical category by repetition. Two more checks fail outright: the chi-square test is reported as p below 0.05 with no statistic and no table, and the risk direction flips inside the chapter, 5.3.1 asserting that low GCI scores mean higher risk while 5.3.3 reports that Russia, Ukraine and the United States 'have higher scores, indicating greater vulnerability', which reverses the index it just defined.

What the chapter actually establishes is worth recording because it is the opposite of what the label says: this declared model chapter contains no model. The span is wrong at both ends: page 8 opens with the Fig.4 caption and the data-filtering prose of the section above, and page 18 runs into '4. Results and Discussion' and stops there, so the declared model chapter ends inside the results. The chapter itself is worth reading because it is the most complete data-preparation record in the F sample: four index formulas for being found, thwarted, causing loss and severity, each written as a ratio over n_it with a binomial loss indicator and a denominator correction that subtracts the suspected and unrated events; a note that annual data hides mid-year policy changes so the analysis goes monthly; a remainder rule that spreads the twelve-month discrepancy by 12 and hands the leftover units out in the order 1, 4, 7, 10, 2, 5, 8, 11, 3, 6, 9, 12; six UNESCO demographic factors with a stated interpolation rule (zeros before the first non-zero value, forward fill after it); a de-duplication of the June 2023 US spike, where 735 near-identical records become 17 distinct events; three correlation coefficients computed and tabulated for six features; and a TimeXer model described entirely in prose - patches, variate-level embeddings, self-attention inside the endogenous variable, cross-attention to the exogenous ones, and learnable global tokens as the bridge. Five checks a reader can run. The de-duplication silently redefines the dependent variable for one month, replacing a count of records with a count of distinct events, and nothing in the text reconciles the two definitions. The claim that Network Server has 'the lowest correlation values, all of which are closest to 0' holds only for Pearson: for Spearman it is 0.177 for Literacy against 0.196 for Server, and for Kendall 0.162 against 0.166, so Literacy is the flattest in two of the three tables. Kendall's tau is compared with Pearson's r and Spearman's rho as if the three sat on one scale, which they do not, tau being bounded at about two-thirds of rho for monotone dependence. The paper keeps Enrollment at +0.321 while dropping Literacy at +0.249 as a data gap, and never remarks that its other education measure, public spending on education, correlates negatively at -0.289, so two education indicators point opposite ways and only one of them is discussed. And the leftover-unit order 1, 4, 7, 10, 2, 5, 8, 11, 3, 6, 9, 12 is given with no reason, so which months receive the imputed unit is arbitrary. One printing defect: the sentence introducing the spike says 'As shown in Figure M', an unreplaced placeholder in the body text rather than in a caption.

Third, the height read reports the gain reversing above roughly 15 m and then recommends building high within 3-6 m, so the branch that motivated the reading is never inside the design range, and the 15 m is glossed as 'possibly the same value of the width', a numeric coincidence offered as a mechanism. On the method side the genetic algorithm is declared without population size, generation count, seeds or repeat runs, and its convergence evidence is two figures of fitness against parameter, and every shape result is closed by fitting a second-order curve 'perfectly' or 'closely' to an ellipse with no residual given - three separate objectives, vertical air, angular momentum and total rotation, all return the same ellipse, which is either the paper's main finding or an artefact of fitting a two-parameter family to a smooth curve, and the paper never asks which. Eight hyphenated artifact keys - height-result, angle-and-radius-result, flat-width-result, course-length-result, twist-result, tradeoff-design-vector, placement-recommendation, alternative-shape-comparison. The span opens mid-equation inside 3.3.5 with 'W p . So we have,' and no sentence above it, and closes on the last row of Table 1, so eight names cover five sections: 3.3.6's four design parameters for question one, the whole mechanical model for question two with its own assumptions, torque figure and compliance matrix, the tradeoff model for question three, six subsections on alternative half-pipe shapes, and the opening of a verification section. What the chapter does: platform height from a cited 11.06 m/s minimum entry speed, hx = v0^2/2g = 6.241 m; velocity resolved into components with alpha_x about delta and alpha_y about 90 minus delta, vy maximised numerically at delta = 51.66 degrees and the radius from rx = hx/(1-cos delta) = 16.44 m; the acceleration trace of Harding et al distilled into a broken line ac = 2.5g - 2.5gt for t below 1 s and zero after, integrated twice to give vmax 23.31 m/s, Smax 19.27 m and wx = Smax cos alpha = 19.18 m; the course length from a0 = DD' sin alpha + 2 rx delta sin alpha + vx tt in four steps, a0 = 22.85 m, times seven flights, ax = 159.95 m; question two from a compliance-matrix beam to theta = chi vs^2 sin 2delta / 2, maximal at delta = 45 degrees with hx unchanged at 6.241 m, rx = 21.3 m and ax = 165.96 m; question three from the borrowed score PS = 3.42 AVA + 0.011 ADR - 1.794, weighted 0.997 and 0.003, delta_t = 51.63 degrees, rx = 16.37 m and ax = 160.19 m; a placement angle of 18 degrees recommended from the literature; and two alternative families compared in words. Five checks follow. First, the whole design is computed at alpha = 5 degrees while section 5.2 recommends 18 degrees within a 15-18 degree band, and since wx = Smax cos alpha and a0 carries sin alpha and cos alpha, the recommended placement invalidates the lengths that were just computed and nothing is recomputed. Second, the tradeoff model has no tradeoff in it: with k2 = 0.003 the compromise angle sits 0.03 degrees from the vertical-air answer across a 6.66 degree gap, the two designs are 16.44 against 16.37 m in radius and 159.95 against 160.19 m in length, and Table 1 prints both columns side by side so the verification section itself shows the third design is the first one to three significant figures - the paper calls this the answer to the tradeoff question and never says the weights killed it. Third, the arithmetic has two slips in one chain: integrating the quoted acceleration over the quoted one second gives 19.23 m where the paper prints 19.27 m, and 19.27 cos 5 degrees is 19.20 m where the paper prints 19.18 m, both under a quarter of a percent but both visible on the same two lines; and ac = 2.5g - 2.5gt subtracts a velocity from an acceleration, which happens to vanish at t = 1 s and is the only reason the broken line closes. Fourth, the same dependence is treated two ways: question one maximises vy = vs sin delta with vs itself a function of delta through the friction and drop terms, while question two maximises chi vs^2 sin 2delta / 2 with vs held constant, so the two optima, 51.66 and 45 degrees, do not come from comparable problems; and question two keeps hx = 6.241 m from question one, so its design is not independent either. The names are a fourth naming habit: not keys and not labels but full imperative clauses with the object spelled out, averaging twelve words each - 'preserve the failed physiological leaf-mass comparison and select the structural route' - which is the longest name style in the sample, and two of them carry two verbs where this ledger records only one job. The chapter is question-driven in the manner of the fourth record but without the labels: four printed questions (why leaves have various shapes, whether leaf shapes minimise overlap, whether leaf shape relates to branching structure, the leaf mass of a tree) each followed by model, data and one or more tables. What it does: opens by saying it will test the models of section 2 for practical accuracy; answers the first question with growth and physiology arguments and no number; runs regression on data 'sourced from the university biological department and ecology labs' and reads Figures 15 and 16 as fitting 'quite well'; declares the transport model verified by a graph comparison against Bell 1991 with Figure 17 shown and nothing read off it; then four error tables for the overlap hypothesis (6.93, 5.00, 7.19 and 4.72 percent), one for the branching hypothesis (6.53 percent), keeps the failed physiological leaf-mass route as failed and takes the structural route, and closes on a crown table with volume, mass and density. Three checks, and the first is decisive against the chapter's own conclusion. Every table is closed by a sentence saying the error is under 7.5 percent, and three of the four error percentages do not reproduce from their own two columns: Table 5 gives 3.78 over 47.22, 8.0 percent, against a printed 6.93; Table 6 gives 1.20 over 20.10, 6.0 percent, against a printed 5.00; Table 7 gives 1.43 over 18.37, 7.8 percent, against a printed 7.19; only Table 8 reproduces exactly, 1.34 over 28.34, 4.72. The closing table is worse: calculated crown volume 0.0857 m3 against a true 0.8021 m3 is an error of 89 percent, printed as 7.12, and the paper then writes 'the error is less than 7.5 percent, which provided sufficient evidence to verify our estimation method'. The same table is internally inconsistent three ways: 41.5178 kg over 0.0857 m3 is 484 kg per m3, not the printed 593; the printed density times the printed volume gives 50.8 kg, not 41.52; and the wood density input of 0.90e3 alone would give 77 kg. Second, the branching table has no true-value column at all - the error is the gap between the model's wind torque 0.0068 and its own gravity torque 0.0063, so the validation is the model checked against itself, and that gap is 7.4 percent, not the printed 6.53. Third, the two middle overlap tables are not comparable: same inputs, one reports a total of 18.90 against a true 20.10 and the other says 'per leaf' with 19.80 against 18.37, so if the second is per leaf the true total is 367 and neither error means anything; and Tables 6 and 7 share identical input columns, so they are the same computation reported twice with different arithmetic. Two smaller notes for reuse: the text points at 'Figure 1 and 2' where the figures are captioned 15 and 16, and the table sequence runs 5 6 7 8 9 11, so Table 10 is missing. note: Seventh results chapter, pages 12-35: 31,429 characters and 3,805 whitespace tokens, 135 sentences, no m-token noise, so one stored name per 423 - but most of that bulk is a sixty-row, six-column leaf-mass table, so the prose per name is very much thinner than the ratio suggests, and this record should not be read as a dense chapter. Nine hyphenated artifact keys, the same family as the first and fifth records, five of them ending in -output, -result or -table. The span is the longest in the sample: it opens on the last seven AHP weights with no sentence above them and runs through the maple classification test, all of Model Two (leaf distribution), all of Model Three (tree profile against leaf shape), all of Model Four (leaf mass) and stops on the Strengths and Weaknesses heading - four models, and each model's own introduction, hypothesis and derivation is inside the results span, so the name list covers four chapters' worth of work with nine names. What the blocks do: AHP weights and consistency; ten measured shape parameters reduced to a seven-term deviation index and six category scores; the maple classified as Category 4; three species' internode and leaf length turned into a predicted latitude; three regressions of leaf shape against tree profile with their F tests; the CO2 route to a leaf-mass table; and the logistic age-size relation closed by asserting a correlation. Five checks. First, and it is the interesting one, all three regressions reproduce: recomputing the least squares from the printed five pairs gives slopes 0.3906, 0.2055 and 0.6567 against printed 0.3905, 0.2055 and 0.6567, intercepts 0.3614, 0.6208 and 0.1900 exactly, r-squared 0.174, 0.798 and 0.965 against printed 0.1783, 0.7985 and 0.9645, and F of 0.63, 11.87 and 82.0 against printed 0.63, 11.8857 and 81.5595 - so this is the first chapter in the branch whose arithmetic survives being recomputed, and the defect is elsewhere. Second, the AHP weights connect to nothing: the deviation index is printed as a sum over I1 to I7, and all six category columns add up to their printed ID exactly, but a plain sum is what reproduces, so the seven weights, the lambda, the CI and the CR are computed and then never used in the classification they were built for. The consistency check also misquotes its own criterion, 'CR < 0.01' where Saaty's threshold is 0.10, and CI = (7.0512 - 7)/6 = 0.0085 against a printed 0.0087. Third, the classification is not a test: the paper says it compared the maple with the six categories and found it resembles Category 4 most, and only then runs the model to confirm, so one leaf, a hypothesis fixed by eye and no held-out case underlie the claim in 5.4 that the model classifies 'any given leaf reliably'. Fourth, the latitude test is an identity plus a typo: tan alpha = h/L is the model's own optimum rearranged, the conversion is alpha to 90 - alpha, and all three predicted latitudes reproduce exactly (38.66, 28.4, 33.69 against printed 38.65, 28.39, 33.69), which means it tests whether real trees sit at the predicted internode ratio and nothing else; the first row's true latitude is printed as '35~35', a zero-width band that excludes the predicted 38.65, so the sentence claiming every prediction falls inside its true range is false on the table's own numbers. The model's definition of alpha is also wrong astronomy - the greatest annual solar altitude is at the solstice, not at the vernal equinox, though the equinox conversion is the one actually used. Fifth, the leaf-mass table prints 360 cells and no intermediate: the CO2 column, the fit statistics for the quadratic that produced it and the units bridge are all absent, and the fit is described as 'actually fit the data perfectly' with no number, while the age-size model is printed with a sign that cannot grow, P = k1 (1 - e^{k2 A}) with positive k2 falling with age and its transform A = k4 ln(1 - k5 P^{k6}) taking the log of a bounded argument. Two smaller notes for reuse: 'According to our study in X.2' and 'our model in X.3' are printed with the placeholder X, and the seventh block's conclusion contradicts itself in one sentence, 'the shape characteristics of tree may not well reflect the tree shape'. One move worth keeping: block 3 ends on the database scope rather than on the success claim, which makes it the first results block in this sample whose limit is deliberate rather than pulled in by a coarse span.

note: Eighth results chapter, pages 15-24: 15,885 characters, 2,432 words, 87 sentences, two m-tokens of noise, so one stored name per 304. Eight hyphenated artifact keys, the fourth record of that family. The span opens mid-sentence on 'SEtotal is [0, 1]' so the definition of the score the whole chapter ranks by is cut off above the heading, and it closes on the last paragraph of section 7, which means the authors' own improvement section, 6.1 to 6.3, is inside the results span and unnamed: three self-declared defects - leaf classification that ignores photosynthesis type, a grid algorithm that cannot tell big leaves apart, a photosynthesis model with one input - collapse into a single name together with the conclusion. What the blocks do: four leaf types scored under three tree profiles and the best one chosen per profile; the poplar figure read with the remark that when theta and phi are small the irradiance is largest; the claim that the hypothesis stands because the results are generally expected; a sample-size limit handed to the reader; a field measurement of thirty-two coordinate systems to pick the simulated tree closest to a real camphor; the mass chain LMA times leaf area; a thirty-point sweep of three crown profiles over height; four regression plots; and a closing bounded interpretation. Five checks. First, the comparison that carries the hypothesis cannot discriminate where it is used: the poplar column reads 0.62, 0.49, 0.63, 0.62, so the chosen shape wins by 0.01, the Japanese banana column reads 0.82, 0.83, 0.82, 0.85, a spread of 0.03, and section 6.2 admits in the authors' own words that for big leaves the grid algorithm 'tends to generate similar results for different leaf shapes' - the paper states the failure of its own discriminator three pages after using it to rank. Second, the verification sentence is 'since the results are generally expected, our hypothesis stands', which is confirmation by expectation rather than by test. Third, the case study transposes a digit in its own input: the average LMA is derived as 177.74 g per m2 and the mass line multiplies 177.47 by 72 m2 to 12,777.84 g, which is exact for the transposed value, so the error is in the input and not the product. Fourth, the scale bridge is a bare factor: the polygon output 150.0359 becomes 6.001436 m2, exactly a division by 25, an unstated length scale of 5, and the leaf is modelled as a rhombus with a longer diagonal of 0.25 in unspecified units against a measured transverse diameter of 5 cm, so the simulation and the tree are never tied together on the page. Fifth, the sweep is miscounted and mislabelled: three profiles at heights from 5 to 10 m in 0.5 m steps is thirty-three simulations and the text says 'the total 30 data', and the sentence says the sweep calculates total leaf area while the regression it feeds is described as leaf mass. On top of those, four regressions are reported with no coefficient, no r-squared and no p value anywhere, and the one quantitative claim made from them, that mass grows cubically with height for similar crown profiles, contradicts the paper's own geometry, since a similar profile makes ground area proportional to height squared. Two notes for reuse. The naming is the artifact-key family again but its keys are process keys rather than object keys - 'case-tree mass chain', 'height-profile sweep', 'profile-stratified regression' - which is the most informative variant of the habit in this branch, because each name says what operation the block performs and a coder can label it without reading the page. And the move worth copying is the unnamed one: section 6 lists the model's defects one by one, each tied to the section it comes from, which is a strength-and-weakness block written as an improvement list rather than as an apology.

Twenty-four names in the layout, but only thirteen curated units carry chapter 'results' in the same artifact (RES-001 to RES-013, pages 10-38), and the layout's own span duplicates the model-establishment span (results 8-39 with 2,182 words, model-establishment 4-39 with 2,224), so this record codes the twenty-four layout blocks and records the thirteen-unit parallel as a coarser annotation of the same pages rather than a rival count. Five checks. First, the crown-solid table contradicts itself under both denominators: the printed means are 1.80, 1.18, 1.09, 0.60, 3.44, 1.75, the fourteen-tree column means are 1.884, 1.198, 1.070, 0.627, 4.199, 1.654, and the thirteen-tree means excluding the one outlier are 1.805, 1.140, 1.023, 0.601, 3.445, 1.751 - so cylinder, cone and pyramid reproduce only at n=13, while the two solids the paper actually selects, paraboloid at a printed 1.09 and vertical ellipsoid at 1.18, reproduce at neither denominator, and the subset that produces the three matching columns is never stated. Third, the leaf mass constant is given as 280 g per cubic centimetre for oak, a mass per volume of crown, so the figure is four hundred times the density of water and three orders out; the fitted exponential attenuation downstream absorbs the scale instead of checking it. Fourth, the logistic discriminant table copies its header from the blade-length table, so a leaf-index table is headed 'mean log (blade length/cm)', and region 1 reads P = 6.261e-02, which does not reject, while the prose says the ratio differs significantly in the two branching patterns. The allometric section reports a quadratic fit at R2 = 0.98 from fourteen trees with three parameters, in-sample and with no DBH column printed anywhere in the chapter or the table of measurements, so the fit is unverifiable from the paper; and the comparison that follows states mean fractions of 0.93 and 1.03, where 0.93 is not the improved model's 1.08 or 1.02 but is a cell value from the fourteenth measurement row. function_strings: decompose the model into packing and heating components; justify regular even-sided polygon candidates and packing families; define geometry cases, two orientations, clearance, and space efficiency; introduce diffusion plus Newton heating and the FTCS numerical route; show why naive grid-overlap surface assignment creates artifacts; show why uniform edge averaging destroys corner contrast; define the angle-based hybrid corner weighting and normalization; define corner-versus-edge heating efficiency; combine spatial and heating efficiencies with the preference weight; hand the final score to shape enumeration
note: Sixth type-A model chapter, pages 4-7, the brownie-pan problem: 15,590 characters, 2,415 words, 55 sentences, so one name per 242. Ten layout paragraph functions against six curated units, the second consecutive paper in this ledger where the two counts disagree, and here the layout's own 1,504 words against 2,415 measured shows why: the span opens above 'The Model' on the Parameters section and closes inside 'Determining Parameters by Experimentation', so the ten names cover about two thirds of the span and the only empirical section, the two baking experiments with a thermocouple and a Styrofoam calorimeter, carries no name at all. Coded 10 blocks: four define, two limit, and one each route, select, derive, handoff. What is worth taking from this chapter is the middle: blocks five and six are two consecutive limit blocks that each reject a candidate method on the page, grid-overlap surface assignment because the grid fall invents edge squares with little surface area and those cells then fail to reach oven temperature, and uniform edge averaging because it also flattens the corners the simulation exists to distinguish, and only then does block seven construct the hybrid corner weight. That is the cleanest reject-then-replace sequence in the A model sample, and the weight it produces satisfies its own stated constraints, 2 at theta = 90 degrees and 1 at theta = 180 degrees, with the derivative falling fastest at 90 and flattening toward 180, exactly as the paragraph asks. Four checks. First, the oven temperature is printed as 350 degrees Celsius in the parameter experiment, which is 662 Fahrenheit, while brownies bake at 350 Fahrenheit; that number is the T_air that enters the transport equation, so a unit slip in the one measured input propagates into every simulated temperature in the paper. Second, the clearance rule is asymmetric: the 8 percent area inflation to 1.08A is applied to squares and to hexagons and to nothing else, while the reason given for it, airflow between pans, is a property of the oven and not of the shape, so the two shapes the hypotheses favour are the two that carry a packing penalty and every larger polygon packs as if air flowed through it. Third, heating efficiency is the mean edge temperature divided by the mean corner temperature over the whole simulation, so two shapes whose corners and edges both approach the oven temperature both score near one, and the ratio therefore measures bake duration as much as geometry; the chapter calls the result a zero-to-one normalised scale and offers no invariance test, and the only parameter sweep in the paper is in the sensitivity chapter. Fourth, the candidate set is fixed before the model can speak: only even-sided polygons are enumerated, the triangle is excluded on the assertion of poor corner heating that the machinery could have measured, and the tessellation check that squares and hexagons receive is replaced after octagons by the assertion that higher polygons are close enough to circles for lattice packing to win. Naming is the full-clause family again, and this is the first record in the branch where two names state an argument rather than an output - both begin 'show why' - which is the honest way to name a rejected method.

function_strings: state transient and steady heat equations; state flux boundary and two-dimensional reduction; name finite-element software and standard parameters; present square and circle fields; compare fixed-area polygons; select edge standard deviation and fit its edge-count relation
note: Seventh type-A model chapter, pages 4-8, the same 2013 brownie-pan problem as the sixth record and a different paper: 8,634 characters, 1,217 words, 68 sentences, two noise tokens, so one name per 203, the tightest model chapter in the A sample. Six names against seven curated units, so here the layout is the coarser of the two. The span also overruns its own list at the bottom: it reaches the first page of Model 2 and the area-utilisation objective, which no name covers, so six names describe a one-model chapter and the span contains the beginning of the second. Coded 6 blocks: two define, and one each route, read-figure, compare, compute. The chapter's shape is the simplest in the sample - one governing equation, its steady limit, a boundary condition, a dimensional reduction, a solver, four parameters, two plots, a polygon sweep, a summary statistic and a fit - and it is the cleanest example of a model chapter that delegates all its arithmetic to software and then quotes four decimals. Four checks. First, the fit is a one-point calibration dressed as curve fitting: the printed relation sigma = 23.605/m^2 + 0.035 reproduces the square's edge deviation 1.5139 almost exactly (1.5103) because 23.605 is what passing the intercept 0.035 through that single row gives, and it then drifts to +17.4 percent at five edges, +24.8 at seven, +30.3 at eight and +68.5 percent at sixteen, so the relation is right where the solver was already right and wrong everywhere the sweep does work. Second, the intercept contradicts the table it was fitted to: as m grows the printed curve tends to 0.035, while the same table prints 0.0000 for the circle, and the sentence above it says the edge deviation approaches zero - the paper keeps the term that makes its story work and drops the constant that does not. Third, the boundary treatment is doubled and mislabelled: convection is written into the volume equation as -lambda laplacian(T) = h(T_ext - T), which turns Newton cooling into an internal source, and then a Neumann flux condition is imposed on the same boundary as well; the flux equation is also called a third-order PDE when it carries only first derivatives. Fourth, the standard state is dimensionally wrong in two of four entries - the flux q0 is given as 1000 W/(s m) where the boundary condition requires W/m^2, and the air temperature is 330 K, which is 57 degrees Celsius, not an oven - and the parameters table has no mesh size, no refinement level and no convergence study, so a statistic printed to four decimals (4.3236) has no discretisation evidence behind it. Naming note: the verbs are state, present, compare, select and fit rather than the single reporting verb of the third record, so this list reads as a procedure rather than as a series of captions - the most writerly of the A model lists so far.

function_strings: positive model-establishment move 1; positive model-establishment move 2; positive model-establishment move 3; positive model-establishment move 4
note: Eighth type-A model chapter, pages 8-10, a highway traffic simulation: 6,115 characters, 953 words, 38 sentences, no noise, so one stored name per 238. This is the first record in the ledger whose stored names carry no content at all - 'positive model-establishment move 1' to 'move 4' - so the four names are placeholders and every job below is assigned from the text in page order; the count of four is still the artifact's own paragraph count and the record is kept in the tallies for that reason, but the naming evidence this branch collects cannot use it. Four blocks: a mechanism block on why every speed converges to a value set by density, then a define block carrying the borrowed PIEV reaction time, the decision loop, the safe gap Gs = Tr*V and the two driving principles, a source block for the acceleration and deceleration probabilities taken from SUN yue 2005 with their two tables, and a define block for the overtaking probability and the two overtaking conditions. Four checks. First, the overtaking probability puts a velocity difference in an exponent, Po = 1 - 0.9 exp(Vmax2 - Vmax1), where the velocities are counted in cells per second, so the exponent carries units and the law cannot be re-scaled; the same expression also returns exactly 0.1 for equal maxima and for any faster vehicle ahead, so a hopeless overtake is attempted as often as an even one, and the sentence that motivates it, 'the larger the difference in velocity, the more likely the vehicle is to accelerate', is about a difference in class maxima rather than in the current speeds, so the quantity that drives the decision is a property of the vehicle type and not of the situation. Second, the safe gap is a reaction distance only, Gs = Tr*V, with no braking term, while the deceleration rule is capped at one cell per second per step and the crash-free rule then permits a stop from any speed; the model therefore contains two incompatible deceleration regimes, a capped one for normal following and an uncapped one that appears only when a crash is imminent, and the crash-free rule is what the later results will be measuring. Third, 'when G < Gs but won't crash if moving forward' is used as a rule condition without any statement of how the won't-crash case is decided, so the branch that selects the rule is undefined at exactly the boundary the safety claim rests on. Fourth, the chapter's opening promise, that the preliminary analysis of convergence speed 'will be justified by later implementation of the model', is the only support offered for the claim that dense traffic moves at the speed of its slowest vehicle. Naming note: with the placeholders present there is nothing to say about this paper's names, and that absence is itself the finding - the field that carries the branch's naming evidence can degrade to a numbered stub, so a clone must never copy a name list without reading the chapter.

function_strings: positive model-establishment rhetorical move 1; positive model-establishment rhetorical move 2; positive model-establishment rhetorical move 3
note: Ninth type-A model chapter, the same page only, 12-12: 2,089 characters, 257 words measured against 360 in the layout, six sentences, no noise, so one stored name per 86, the thinnest chapter in the ledger. Second consecutive paper whose names are stubs - 'positive model-establishment rhetorical move 1' to 'move 3' - and here the stub field is not an isolated accident, because the neighbouring model-improvement chapter, pages 12-15 with 1,520 words and 17 blocks, carries the same stub form, so this paper's artifact names are unusable throughout and the jobs below come from reading the page. Coded 3 blocks: two define and one route. What the page contains is method framing and nothing else: AHP defined as a method that quantifies subjective factors and, through consistency checking, minimises the deviation those factors introduce; a pointer to the index hierarchy figure; then grey relation analysis, the max entropy model and a concept called the grey relation depth coefficient introduced as new and put to improve the model, with no formula, no units and no statement of what it is. That makes this record the first in the A sample where the model-establishment label covers a framing page and the algebra sits in the next chapter - the label is not wrong about position, since section 5.3 does come before 5.4, but it is wrong about content, and any count of chapter length that trusts the label will read this chapter as three blocks of model. Four checks. First, the sentence that introduces the hierarchy figure is broken and points at the wrong number, 'the following Index Hierarchy Relationship Figure is displayed in Figure As is vividly shown in Figure 2' against a caption reading Figure 3. Second, the AHP claim is a misstatement of the method: consistency checking measures whether the pairwise judgements are internally coherent, it cannot reduce the deviation caused by subjectivity, so the sentence promises reliability the procedure does not deliver. Third, the grey relation depth coefficient is the only original construct announced on the page and it is announced without a definition, which leaves the next chapter's objective weights resting on a term the reader has not been given. Fourth, at 257 words and six sentences for three named blocks, the chapter cannot be carrying a model at all, and the transferable lesson is about labelling: a model chapter that only cites methods is a literature paragraph wearing a chapter heading.

function_strings: overtaking relation; choice diagram; initial transition; iterative update; limit argument; numerical setup; numerical match; light-boundary handoff; heavy failure mechanism; safe-distance constraint
note: Tenth type-A model chapter, pages 7-11, the keep-right rule: 13,513 characters, 1,868 words, 74 sentences, no noise, so one name per 187. Ten short noun-phrase keys, two and three words each - overtaking relation, iterative update, limit argument, heavy failure mechanism - which is the noun-phrase family of the second results record and the shortest names in the ledger, and each one is a stage of a proof rather than an output. Coded 10 blocks: three derive, two read-figure, and one each define, compute, limit, mechanism, source. The chapter's real subject is a Markov chain: overtaking probabilities set as proportions of speed gaps, a Bayes step that builds the first transition matrix, a matrix update, a bound and a squeeze theorem that kill State 1, the two-state residue that makes State 3 absorbing, a numeric run, and then the boundary where the whole construction stops applying. Four checks. First, the notation reverses the model: 'for i > j, we have vi < vj' makes State 1 the slowest car, so p1 = p(v1 - v2) is negative for every positive p, and all three overtaking probabilities in 3.2.2 come out negative; the matrix, the weighted-average row sum and the absorbing-state result only work with v1 > v2 > v3, which is what the paper's own sentence about State 3 as the lowest speed says. One printed inequality contradicts the algebra that follows it, and nothing downstream notices. Second, the numerical match is a rounding presented as attainment: with the paper's own numbers, p1 = 0.35, p2 = 0.45, p3 = 0.29 from an initial (0.2, 0.5, 0.3), the iteration gives (0.0013, 0.0006, 0.9981) at six transitions, not (0, 0, 1), so the figure's equality is two-decimal rounding; the text then calls it consistent with the model and adds that the result will be tested again in 3.5, which is a test declared passed before it is run. Third, the limit proof needs max(p1, p2) < 1, that is p times a speed gap below one, while p is only constrained to be positive; the bound is asserted and then satisfied by the particular numbers chosen for the run, which is why the proof reads as validated. Fourth, the two-second rule is applied as 2v3 for cars in State 3 only, although the queue it is protecting is a mix of states, and the heavy-traffic mechanism - no return to the right lane, cars pile up on the left - is asserted from a picture rather than derived, after which the section concludes that the danger index is lowest in heavy traffic because there is no overtaking, which reverses the chapter's own logic that non-overtaking is what makes traffic slow. One assumption to carry: overtaking is declared instantaneous on the page - 'we arbitrarily ignore the accelerating process' - and that jump is what lets the transition matrix exist at all.

function_strings: discrete representation; particle-hopping choice; local update; lane permission; output definition; continuum route; single-lane PDE; two-lane extension; lane exchange; steady state
note: Eleventh type-A model chapter, pages 5-19, the keep-right rule modelled twice: 26,180 characters, 3,701 words, 136 sentences, no noise after dropping the running headers, so one name per 370 - but that figure is span-inflated and should not be quoted as a tight chapter, because the layout span runs over 3.1.2 and 3.1.3, the parameter table and the whole discrete results discussion with Figures 3 to 10, which the separate results chapter also claims. Ten noun-phrase keys, two words each and the same family as the fourteenth record, and they divide cleanly into a discrete half (representation, hopping family, local update, lane permission, output definition) and a continuum half (continuum route, single-lane PDE, two-lane extension, lane exchange, steady state). Coded 10 blocks: four define, three derive, and one each select, route, source. Five checks. First, the two models never meet: the discrete half is fully parameterised (L = 2048 sites, T = 4096 steps, Pd = 0.1, Pc = 0.7, Vmax 5 and 3) and the continuum half borrows eleven parameters from a citation (Tm = 10 s, uf = 30 m/s, a = 0.01, b = 5, c0 = 10 m/s, rho_m = 0.14 veh/m, r1 = 150 m2/s, r2 = 50 m2/s, rho_c = 0.05 veh/m, E = 100), and nothing converts a site into a metre, so the two flow curves are drawn for the same road and never compared. Second, the safety index points both ways: the text says safety is proportional to drivers' reaction time and that a longer reaction time is safer, while the formula averages exp(-gap/speed) over cars and steps, which falls as the gap grows, and the paper then says a larger value means more danger - the words and the sign of the formula disagree, and the exponent is a time, so exp carries units. Third, the energy cost derivation drops its own terms: the kinetic-energy difference is factored into (V(t) - V(t-1)) times (V(t) + V(t-1)) and then the first factor and the one half disappear, which is only legitimate if every speed change is exactly plus one, while the update rules also allow a drop to gap - 1 and a further random decrement. Fourth, the simulation procedure contradicts the definition it is meant to compute: the definition divides the accumulated safety sum by N times T, the table's step 17 divides it by Q, and the step list jumps from 11 to 13 with step 12 missing. Fifth, the weighted objective is justified by an independence claim the paper itself refutes one page earlier, where it notices that the flow peak and the safety peak fall at nearly the same density because both are tied to average velocity; the same function normalises by three unexplained constants, 1.2 for flow, 800 for energy and 0.4 for the safety scale, and those constants set the trade-off as much as the weights do. Naming note: the ten names are a clean table of contents for a two-model chapter, which is the most useful thing this record adds - discrete half first, continuum half second, and the reader can see the paper's structure without opening it.
