note: Twelfth type-A model chapter, pages 6-8, the KRP rule on a two-lane cellular automaton. Device for this record: the layout reports 736 words and 8 paragraph functions over a span that actually holds 1,189 words and 14 paragraphs of more than eight words, so the eight names are not a rival segmentation of the same content, they are a partial annotation that stops at the end of 4.2.1. The uncovered tail is real prose and real model content: 4.2.2 sets the physical scale (one step one second, one site 7.5 m, 133 sites, 997.5 m loop, empty-or-occupied), the initial population, and four parameters; 4.2.3 then defines flow, density, average speed and lane-change frequency. So the density for this chapter is 85 words per paragraph, not 92, and the annotation cannot be used to argue that a model chapter is short. Coded the eight stored names: four define, two select, one limit, one mechanism, with the fifth block closing on a handoff because it ends by dispatching to the KRP, KROL and HLLR rule sets rather than by completing a definition. What this chapter does better than most A model chapters is state the update machinery and its own physical implausibility in the same breath: the lateral sub-step is called unfeasible because vehicles cannot move purely sideways, and the text says the pair of sub-steps is what makes sense physically. It also distinguishes parallel from sequential updates and says the two give slightly different results, which most A papers leave unstated. Three defects. First, vthreshold enters the simulation setup with the value 4 before it is defined, and it is defined only inside the KROL section pages later, so a reader meeting the setup has a parameter with no meaning and no unit. Second, the single random braking probability in the setup does not match the model, whose S3 draws rand against a per-vehicle pd(i). Third, the results agenda announces six factors including the proportion of large vehicles, but the model has no vehicle-type field at all: every vehicle occupies one 7.5 m site and has only a desired speed, so that factor has no variable to act on. Fairness note: the metric formulas on page 8 come through the text layer as broken glyphs, so the flow and density definitions are recorded as unverified rather than as wrong.

function_strings: state definition; acceleration; safe braking; randomization; position update; single-lane boundary
note: Thirteenth type-A model chapter, page 3, and the second record whose chapter label does not match its content (the first is P-A-2014-26911). The tag says model-establishment but the text is section 2.2, a citation-backed restatement of the Nagel-Schreckenberg rules: the paper's own model begins at 3.2 on page 5, which the layout tags model-improvement. So this is a source chapter in the model slot, and it is coded that way - one source block, four define blocks for the four rules, one limit block that states the single-lane scope and announces the modification. Measured 453 words against a 426-word layout claim, close enough, but the six names are finer than the prose: only four paragraphs exceed eight words, because each rule is a numbered one- or two-line item. Three defects, one of which is the kind that changes results. First, acceleration is conditioned on having more than v+1 empty cells ahead, where Nagel-Schreckenberg needs the gap to exceed the current speed; with d = v+1 the car here does not accelerate and never reaches that speed, which systematically depresses speed in exactly the gap-limited regime that decides flow. The same sentence is repeated verbatim in the implementation's step 1, so it is the model rather than a typo. Second, the braking step says the car reduces its velocity to x, a symbol defined nowhere, while the formula beside it says min{d, v}. Third, the chapter carries no physical scale at all: no cell length in metres and no time-step length, and the results keep the same convention, reporting Vmax as 6 and 2 cells per time step and flow in cars per step, so nothing in the paper can be compared with a real traffic count. Positive: the final paragraph is an honest scope statement - the model is single lane and cannot answer a lane-change question without modification - and the claim that the original randomization can never create an accident is true for the original rules and is explicitly used to motivate the paper's modified randomization.

note: Fourteenth type-A model chapter, pages 8-10, an Ebola SEIR model, and the third record with stub names - the single stored name is the word setup. It is also the only one of the three whose counts are wrong, so the whole units artifact for this paper has collapsed: this chapter claims 96 words where the span holds 680, and the introduction claims 160 words for pages 3-5, which hold 1,167. I therefore coded the span by hand at my own grain and recorded eleven paragraphs over eight words, of which eight are model work and three are 4.1.3 result paragraphs (the dotted-curve description and the fits very well sentence) that I left to the results branch rather than letting read-figure and compare blocks inflate a model chapter. Coded 8 blocks: three define, two source, two route, one limit, with block six closing on a handoff. Two things are done well. R0 = beta/gamma with 1/gamma = 5.61 days reproduces Table 1 exactly - 1.51, 2.53 and 1.59 over 5.61 give 0.269, 0.451 and 0.283, which are the printed 0.27, 0.45 and 0.28 - and both borrowed durations carry citations, the 5.61-day infectious period to Chowell and the 5.3-day incubation to the 1995 Congo outbreak. Two things are not. Equation 4.1 has five compartments and not one of them is a death variable, yet two paragraphs in this span promise the estimated number of cases and deaths and the figure plots a deaths curve beside a model curve, so the second output has no equation behind it anywhere in the paper. And the control decay rate k is 0.048 for all three countries although the transmission rates differ by 70 percent, 0.27, 0.45 and 0.28, which means one control schedule is shared by three epidemics with different interventions; no page justifies the sharing. Chapter label note: the tag covers pages 8-10, which run from the tail of the SEIR equations through the data, the parameter table and the whole first fit, so it overlaps both the data-preprocessing and results tags for the same paper. Do not use this paper's layout counts for any density statistic.

note: Fifteenth type-A model chapter, pages 7-9, an Ebola multi-layer stochastic epidemic model, and the fourth stub-name record: one stored name, the word setup, claiming 108 words for a span that holds 1,341. Coded by hand at 15 blocks, six define, three route, two mechanism, two limit, one select, one source, with block eleven closing on a mechanism. This is a different species of model chapter from the other fourteen and the one worth copying for a problem whose model is a simulation rather than a system of equations: it opens with modelling objectives rather than with symbols (aim split into spread and treatment, then three reasons the split is hard), then defines the problem space through boundary assumptions, then chooses the framework and describes the layers from the bottom up, and only then, in 2.3.1, reaches its first equation. That order - aims, scope, framework, layers, algebra - is the honest order for a stochastic simulation, where the algebra is a rule table rather than a system. Three things to carry forward. The chapter's only equation in the span is Pinteract = count of that type in the region divided by total individuals in the region, which is a frequency, not a model, and it is presented as the interaction law; a clone should either derive that ratio or call it an assumption. The framework is called a relatively recent approach with no citation in the sentence that adopts it, so the one literature claim that would justify the architecture arrives unsourced. And the scope is declared for three countries while the parameter set is normalised to Sierra Leone and Liberia because Guinea lacks statistics - disclosed on the next page of the same chapter and again in the limitations, where the paper says Guinea and Liberia share propagation parameters. That is honest but strategically placed: the scope sentence comes first, the caveat after. Density note: with the layout collapsed, this chapter's name and word counts must not enter any density statistic; the hand count gives 89 words per block.

function_strings: setup; method
note: Sixteenth type-A model chapter, pages 9-10, a six-compartment Ebola model, and the fifth stub-name record: two stored names, setup and method, 102 words claimed against 594 measured. Coded five blocks: three define, one mechanism, one route. This is the most economical real model chapter in the A sample so far and the best template of the four-part shape - announce the model as a figure, name the compartments, write the system, then explain each flow in words - because the system here is short enough to be checked by eye. The balance holds: dS = -(beta_I I1 + beta_2 I2 + beta_F F) S, dE = the same inflow minus sigma E, dI1 = sigma E - gamma1 I1, dI2 = delta1 gamma1 I1 - gamma2 I2, dF = delta2 gamma2 I2 - gamma_F F, and dR returning both recovery streams, so the six equations sum to minus gamma_F F and the population shrinks by burials only, which is a deliberate and defensible closure. The cumulative outputs are also consistent with the system, yC = the integral of sigma E and yD = the integral of delta2 gamma2 I2, and this is the paper where the death count actually has an equation behind it, unlike P-A-2015-32150. One defect, and it is arithmetic rather than rhetoric: all six state variables are introduced as fractions of the population, and nothing ever multiplies by a population size, yet yC and yD are fitted against absolute case and death counts from the WHO website. Either a population size is implicit and never written, or every printed case count is off by that factor. One style finding worth keeping: the mechanism block carries an emotional appeal inside the model, the paragraph about holding a dying mother's hand before the body is sprayed with chlorine, and it is doing real argumentative work - it is the justification for letting the dead stay infectious - so the flourish is not decoration but the reason the F compartment exists.

function_strings: setup; method; evidence; qualification
note: Seventeenth type-A model chapter, pages 5-23, the largest span in the ledger: 5,654 words, 19 pages, four stored names, 136 words claimed. Because the span is the whole modelling body of the paper I coded it at section level, 20 blocks, 283 words per block: seven define, five derive, two route, two source, two compute, one interpret, one limit. The chapter is a stack of five models in a row - SEIR, SEIIR, SEIIR with medication, a set-covering facility model, and a logistic drug-production and delivery model - and the transitions between them are the most useful thing in it, because each one names what the previous model could not do (SEIR has no isolation, so SEIIR; medication cures only early patients, so M(t); drug supply is short, so a delivery system). Six checks, all from the printed pages. First, the closure contradicts itself: N = S + E + I + R with assumption 8 fixing N, and then dD = f gamma I accumulates deaths that are counted nowhere in N, so either N falls every day or the four-state sum exceeds N. Second, the death term is mislabelled in words: the text says (1 - f) gamma I is the number of deaths per day and the equation immediately below gives dR = (1 - f) gamma I, that is the same quantity as recoveries. Third, f1 and f2 are swapped between sentence and equation: the prose says the mortality of isolated patients f1 is much lower than the non-isolated f2, while the equations apply f1 to I_free and f2 to I_isolated, and the simulation then sets f1 = 0.8 above f2 = 0.6, which is the opposite of the assumption the chapter leans on. Fourth, M(t) enters dR and dD with the same sign and leaves dI_isolated, so each medicated patient both recovers and dies and the total population grows by M(t) per unit time. Fifth, the eight evaluation norms become five columns in Table 4: economy, education and age are defined in prose, are absent from the district table, and appear only at country level in Table 5, so the district h values that drive the facility model are computed from five of the eight promised factors. Sixth, the new density A_n = a1 b1 + a2 b2 + ((a2 - a1)/a2) b3 never receives values for b1, b2, b3, which are only constrained to sum to one, so the one index the chapter rewrites cannot be reproduced. Two more for the language file: humidity is introduced with the sentence 'The temperature of the area is C_n', a copy of the temperature line, and the whole chapter calls population density pollution density (R_n is the pollution of area n) and medical centres mental centres ('seven mental centers', 'the scope that every mental center manages'). Cross-paper note: this paper's Table 1 gives transmission rates 0.27, 0.43 and 0.29 with the same Chowell citation that P-A-2015-32150 uses for 0.27, 0.45 and 0.28, and its fatality column 0.75, 0.49, 0.69 is never used by the sub-models, which set f1 and f2 by hand.

function_strings: setup; method; evidence; qualification; handoff
note: Eighteenth type-A model chapter, pages 4-6, an Ebola model written twice, as a stochastic event process and as a deterministic difference system. Six stored names, 160 words claimed, 1,652 words in the span, of which the first 557 are the tail of the assumptions chapter that the layout also tags separately, so the model content is about 950 words in seven blocks: three define, one route, one mechanism closing on a check, one derive, one compare. This is the most rigorous stochastic specification in the A sample and the chapter to copy when the answer needs a simulation: eight labelled outcomes of one timestep with an explicit probability for each, a stated validity condition that the eight probabilities sum to at most one so that no timestep carries two events, and then a Monte Carlo procedure described in three sentences - draw a uniform, find the cumulative interval, increment a counter. Table 3 then says which model earns its place, randomness and integer populations on one side, analytical steady state and speed on the other. One verified defect, and it is the kind that only a side-by-side read finds. The rate symbols are lost from the text layer, so I read equation (3) from the rendered page 6: P_{n+1} = P_n(1 + eps - phi - nu - alpha I_n) + eps H_n, I_{n+1} = I_n(1 + eps - gamma - beta) + alpha I_n P_n, H_{n+1} = H_n(1 - phi) + beta I_n + nu P_n. The infected equation keeps its own birth term eps I_n, so births are being counted - but the vulnerable equation takes births only from H_n, while the stochastic specification defines p1 with the rate applied to H_n + P_n and the prose repeats that all healthy people give birth to vulnerable offspring. The deterministic model is therefore not the expectation of the stochastic one on this one event, and the sum of the three equations drifts by eps(H + I) - phi(P + H) - gamma I instead of the balanced eps(H + P + I) - phi(P + H) - gamma I. Everything else in (3) maps cleanly: nu leaves P and enters H, alpha takes P in both equations, beta and gamma split the infected outflow. Second finding, cross-paper and not an error of this chapter alone: the assumptions list states that Ebola is transferred between living people and that ignoring corpse transmission does not affect the overall rate. `P-A-2015-34317` spends a whole mechanism block arguing the opposite and gives the dead a compartment, and `P-A-2015-32150` adds corpses in its improved model for the same reason. Three A papers, two incompatible positions on the single largest transmission route, each stated without argument.

function_strings: method; method
note: Nineteenth type-A model chapter, page 6, the bathtub paper, and the smallest tagged span in the ledger: 308 words measured against 70 claimed, two stored names that are the same word twice, method and method. Coded two blocks, one define and one select closing on a handoff. The chapter itself is a clean two-move opening that a clone should keep: first the object is fixed as a rectangular prism with named dimensions, six faces, an axis convention, a faucet at x = 0 and a drain at x = L, and one physical closure - the tub is full, so inflow equals overflow; then the reduction is chosen and defended in one paragraph, heat transfer and flow only along x, uniform temperature on each yz cross-section, with the explicit promise that extensive properties keep their three-dimensional character and that the details appear with each model development. That promise is the move worth copying, because the reduction is stated as a decision with retained effects rather than as an approximation to be forgotten. The artifact is the finding rather than the prose. This paper has the worst chapter map in the sample: the layout tags pages 1, 3, 5, 6, 14, 22, 24, 28, 40, 42, 44 and leaves pages 7 to 13 untagged, and those pages hold chapter 3 Thermodynamic Considerations and chapter 4, that is the specific heat, density, conductivity, the Grashof and Reynolds classification of the convection, the parameter table and the energy-balance ODE. In other words the two chapters that actually establish this paper's model carry no tag at all, while model-establishment is given to a two-paragraph geometry page. Reading this paper by its labels would reproduce the preface and skip the model. Two details of the geometry page are still worth a check when cloning: the overflow closure is called equal volumes, which is right for water but it silently fixes the tub as full at all times, so no filling transient exists; and the cross-section element is drawn with volume W H dx, which fixes the cross-section as rectangular, so the later equations cannot represent anything a sealant or a bather would change.

note: Twentieth type-A model chapter, pages 6-10, sections 5 and 5.2, a finite-element heat conduction model of a bathtub written out in full: Fourier's law, the integral energy balance with a source and an outflow, the reduction to a single PDE, a partition of the closed surface into water-air and water-wall, a Robin condition on the air side, insulation on the wall side, a uniform initial condition, and the assembled system. Its eighteen names are content-specific rather than a two-word vocabulary, so the count is usable without re-segmentation, but the mix is off in two places worth recording: there is no name for the fifth-assumption bullet that turns the bather into two spliced cuboids, and there is a name, handoff, with no prose behind it, since the chapter ends on the where list of equation (13). The prose it counts is eighteen paragraphs once the five where-lists are set aside. 1,265 words claimed, 1,821 measured on the pages, but the excess is the display equations and the five where-lists, so the prose claim is close. Three verified defects. First, symbol drift in the finals: equation (7) writes the source as (Tr - Tc) Vp / V_Omega and equation (13) writes the same quantity as f = (Tr - Tc) Vp / Vs, and Vs appears nowhere in the where list, which defines V_Omega and Vp; one of the two denominators is a typo and the reader cannot tell which, in the one equation a clone would copy. Second, the definition of F is dimensionally overclaimed: the prose says F is the heat released per unit time per unit volume, but equation (6) gives F = c rho (Tr - Tc), which has no time in it and is an energy per unit volume; the time only enters later through Vp, so the sentence and the formula disagree about the unit. Third, the insulation step says the wall is insulated and therefore equation (9) becomes (11), but (9) is the air boundary and the wall is (10); one equation too far, in the step that drops a whole boundary condition. Also worth noting for style: the symbol lambda is the thermal conductivity of water and lambda_1, lambda_2 are the film coefficients to air and to the tub, so the same letter carries three meanings subscripted apart, and the Robin condition reads lambda_1 T + lambda dT/dn1 = lambda_1 T1. The one paragraph worth copying whole is 5.1: regularity, material, and the person as two cuboids, three one-line stipulations, each with its reason attached, no discussion.

note: Twenty-first type-A model chapter, section 4 Model Overview plus section 5, and the clearest split in the A sample between what the model is and what the numbers are. Section 4 announces the whole paper in five short blocks: three goals, the simple sub-model, the complicated sub-model, two criteria, and a process figure. Section 5 then does the work the tags call equations, mean and capacity: the continuity, Navier-Stokes and energy equations are quoted from a reference with one sentence of interpretation each, the mean bath temperature is defined by a heat balance qm cp dt = Q and the claim that the field is nearly uniform, cited to another paper, and the heat capacity is built as Newton cooling for the free surface plus a four-resistance series for the insulated wall. Then parameters, substitution, and a seven-step CFD workflow in Gambit and Fluent with the mesh count, iteration count and residual curve. Two artifact notes. First, the names are section-level while the prose is paragraph-level: 5.1.1 alone holds more than ten paragraphs; I coded the thirteen section-level blocks the names describe rather than re-segmenting. Second, the tagged span stops at page 14 but three of its own names, substitution, workflow and field-result, land on pages 15 and 16, so the tag ends two pages before its content does; measured 1,802 words on pages 7 to 14 against 1,720 claimed, so the annotation is close and the boundary is the defect. The arithmetic gives three verified defects, and all three are in the parameter-to-result step. First, the tub dimensions and the tub volume cannot both be true: a b c = 1.8 x 0.9 x 0.64 = 1.037 m3, that is 1,037 litres, against a stated volume of 0.32 m3 and a mass of 320 kg which at 992 kg/m3 is 0.323 m3, so the dimension line in Table 2 disagrees with the capacity by a factor of 3.2 and only the volume agrees with the mass. Second, the areas inherit the error and then stop matching the heat: A1 = 1.05 m2, while the top of that tub is 1.62 m2, and A2 = 2.24 m2 while its four walls are 3.46 m2; recomputing, 10 x 1.05 x 18 gives exactly the tabulated 189.00 W and 10 x 1.62 x 18 gives 291.6 W, so the heat result is consistent with the area and inconsistent with the geometry, which means the dimensional triple is decorative. Third, the mass flow is right in value and wrong in unit: qm = 232.47 / (4174 x 4) = 0.0139 kg/s, which is 0.836 kg per minute, so the text's own gloss of 0.84 kg/min is correct while the table and the sentence both label the figure grams per second, a factor of a thousand. Also worth recording: Table 2 lists h1 twice, at 10 and at 300, where the second row is h2, and the notation table gives density in kg/m2 and the tub size in m3. The chapter is the best example in the A sample of a results section that starts with a parameter table and a substitution step rather than with a figure, and of an honest admission of why simulation replaced solving: the prose says the N-S equation is coupled to the energy equation and quotes the Clay Institute prize as evidence that solving it is out of reach. Fifth defect, and the one a reader would actually notice: the paper disagrees with itself about its own flow rate. The basic model computes 0.014 kg/s, the improvement uses 0.61 kg/s per heating cycle and prints one line as 40.61 kg/s, where formula (38) with T1 = 180 s gives 0.6099, the recommendation at the end tells the bather to add water at 0.03 kg/s, and the memo offers 0.16 kg/s. Five values in one paper for the single number that carries the answer, and the headline recommendation is twice the number its own basic model derived.

note: Twenty-second type-A model chapter, chapter 4 The Model, printed pages 5 to 19, which are file pages 8 to 22, and the sixth and last of the confirmed stub-name artifacts. The stored layout gives three names and the word method three times, puts model-establishment at printed page 5 with 240 words and model-improvement at printed page 17 with 320 words. The first page is right, since chapter 4 does open on printed page 5, and the second is right, since 4.2 opens on printed page 17; what is wrong is the extent, one page each where the chapter runs from printed page 5 to 33, and the count, 240 words where the chapter holds thousands. Measured on printed pages 5 to 19, chapter 4 through 4.2.2, 5,025 words, coded eight section-level blocks. This is the most ambitious establishment chain in the A sample and the most instructive failure. The chain: roadmap, then a differential equation for the water heat assembled from six named terms, then a three-stage decomposition of the bath in time, then a conduction PDE for the field with four Neumann conditions and a point source at the tap, then a universal model in which every term is closed by substituting T = T-bar(t) - K(t) y, then a forced convection cell Fk = Sk Vk for the effect of the bather moving, then a mixing rate f(Fk). Three verified defects. First, the universal model contradicts its own boundary conditions: 4.1.3 imposes Robin conditions on the four side faces of the tub, -lambda dT/dx = h[T - T0] and the same in y and z, but the closed form used in 4.1.4 says the temperature varies only in y; with no x or z dependence the left sides of those conditions are zero, so every side face is forced to sit at air temperature. Second, the model is left with an unknown function in it: the gradient K(t) is described on page 16 as an unknown function of time and the text says that if time permits it will be fitted into a simple function, so the final model cannot be evaluated as printed, and every later strategy inherits that hole. Third, the mixing rate is over-parameterised then collapsed to one parameter: f(Fk) = 1 - exp(-((Fk - Fa)/Fb)^2) is introduced with Fa and Fb both to be determined, then f(0) = 0 is said to force Fa = 0, which leaves only Fb and makes the three-regime description of the sensitivity, insensitive then rapid then saturating, a property of one constant. Artifact lesson, and the reason this paper anchors the stub rule: the same three word layout, method three times, is applied to assumptions, to model-establishment and to model-improvement, and in each case it records the opening page and one page's worth of words, so the artifact cannot say what the chapter does and cannot say how big it is. Nearby prose worth copying anyway: 4.1.2's stage decomposition is real structure, three stages defined by whether the tub is filling, full and still, or full and refilling, each with its own volume law and its own list of terms to keep or drop, and that pattern is exactly what a bath-paper clone needs; but note that stage 2 drops both the inflow and the overflow term without saying they cancel, while stage 3 keeps both in the same full-tub situation, so the same physics is treated two ways in adjacent paragraphs.

note: Twenty-third type-A model chapter, chapter 4, printed pages 6 to 16, the BWOP model, that is the tub without a person in it, and the third distinct placeholder family in the artifact set: every name in every chapter of this paper is the same instruction string, route, derive, compare, interpret, or hand off, repeated as many times as there are paragraphs. A census over all 435 artifacts finds this string family in exactly one paper, this one, in every one of its thirteen chapters, so it is a single-artifact failure rather than a vocabulary habit, and it is invisible to the setup-and-method census that found the 2014 to 2016 A group. The layout also claims six paragraphs and 528 words for pages 7 to 17, where the chapter holds 2,818 words in twelve blocks; nothing in the layout can be used. The chapter itself is the most systematic heat-transfer build in the A sample, and its shape is worth copying whole: define the tub without a person as two processes, heating and dissipation, then compute the two surface coefficients from standard correlations rather than assume them, then the two dissipation paths, then the addition path through the tube with its own wall and its own internal correlation, then simulate what cannot be closed analytically, then read the simulation. Two verified defects. First, radiation is dismissed twice on a wrong argument: 4.2 drops the radiative loss at the water surface on the ground that the surface temperature is low, while at 43 C water under 25 C air the radiative term is about 113 W per square metre at an emissivity of 0.95, against a convective term of 90 at h = 5 and 180 at h = 10, so the discarded term is larger than the kept one at the lower coefficient and comparable at the higher; the sentence would only be right if it had said the two are of the same order, which is the opposite of a reason to drop one. Second, the equation numbering slips in the sentence that closes the governing system: the text says equations (4.19) to (4.23) form the governing equations, while the continuity, momentum and energy equations are (4.20) to (4.24), so one equation too few, in the sentence a reader uses to know what the model consists of. Also worth recording, because it is a check this corpus rarely passes: Table 3 gives cubage 0.3 m3 with height 0.4 m and top 1.4 by 0.7 against bottom 1.0 by 0.5, and the frustum volume from those numbers is 0.296 m3, so the geometry is internally consistent, unlike P-A-2016-44398 whose dimension line missed its own volume by a factor of three. The unit handling is the weak point of the results: Table 4 reports a maximum of 318.0238 K and the prose calls it 318 degrees and then compares 45 degrees against a 55 degree bearing limit in the same breath, so kelvin and celsius are mixed inside one argument, and the volume-average conversion 313.1946 K to 40.4178 C implies an offset of 272.78 rather than 273.15. Finally the chapter carries a naming drift that a clone should not copy: the object is called a cube, a tube and a frustum on adjacent pages, and the where lists define the thickness and inside area of the cube while the simulations of 4.4 use the tapered tub of Table 3.

note: Twenty-fourth type-A model chapter, chapter 4 Simulating Heat Transfer, file pages 7 to 15, printed pages 5 to 13, and a fourth placeholder family: all sixteen stored names are the string derivation or model handoff paragraph plus an ordinal, and the same paper uses controlled scenario or synthesis paragraph plus an ordinal for all twenty names of its sensitivity chapter. A structural census over the 435 artifacts separates this from a naming convention that looks similar and is not: six 2019 and 2020 A papers carry a suffix, dash, visual paragraph plus an ordinal, on top of a content-specific name, so their names are usable and only the suffix is noise, whereas here the ordinal is the whole name. Pages 7 to 15 measure 2,183 words against 1,500 claimed and 14 prose blocks against 16 claimed. The chapter is the best example in the A sample of calibrating a parameter instead of assuming it, and the clearest case of the calibration being thrown away at the last step. The good part: the cooling law is derived from Newton with separation of variables shown line by line, then three published beaker data sets are fitted with the asymptote forced to the room temperature rather than to zero, the fit is refused as insufficient for a tub, a bathtub experiment is run to supply k, k is then modelled as a function of volume and exposed area with the dimensional argument written out, four candidate transforms are compared by R-squared, the best is chosen, and only then does the model get its final form. That is a calibration ladder a clone can follow. The three defects are all at the top of the ladder. First, the exponent is mistaken for the amplitude: equation (14) reads k = 0.3854 exp(-0.1671 (V^2/SA^3)^(1/3)), and the text then says this model predicts a k of 0.385387 for the standard tub and writes dT/dt = -0.385387 T, that is it takes the prefactor as if the exponential factor were one, while the tub's own measured k was 0.00448 per minute, a factor of 86 apart, and the paper's own table puts that k at 0.000075 per second, the same 0.0045 per minute. So the model that was fitted to four points is evaluated at the wrong end of its own curve. Second, the exposed area of a beaker is halved: equation (11) gives SA = 2 pi r^2 + pi r h for an open cylinder, where an open cylinder is pi r^2 + 2 pi r h, so the side surface is divided by two and the base counted twice, and every k in the table inherits it. Third, the symbol T carries two meanings one equation apart: in (16) it is the change in temperature, in (17) it is the absolute temperature of the incoming water in kelvin, and the heat contribution is written dm/dt Cp T_hot, which is a heat rate only if T means a difference. Also worth recording: the fifth row of the k table is per second while the first three are per minute, so the four points entering one regression are not in one unit; and the area column is headed SA in metres rather than square metres.

note: Twenty-fifth type-A model chapter, chapter 5 Model Theory, file pages 7 to 13, printed pages 5 to 11, and the most informative naming in the A sample so far: nine names, one per paragraph, each a content-written sentence saying what the paragraph does and why, motivate the multi-objective structure, translate the proximity principle into demand-weighted objectives, remove the fixed decision-independent term, define an operational bound by naming both limits, map latent demand to observable proxies, build a safety proxy and extend it to cascades, explain the compensation mechanism, combine the benefit channels. I coded by those names. A correction to my first draft of this note: the shape is not unique to this paper. Checked over all 435 artifacts, a model-chapter name of the form verb plus content plus purpose, the shape these nine have, appears in at least 181 papers and is the only name shape in 10 of them, A 6 and B 4, so paper 29 sits at the content-written end of a continuum whose other end is a bare verb template, and the census should say so rather than call this an only case; the check is a verb-list match and the count moves by about fifteen papers depending on the verb list, so only the order of magnitude is solid. Coverage: the artifact claims 2,320 words over pages 7 to 13 where I measure 2,177, and nine names against eleven blocks, because the names stop at the 5.2 objective and neither the 5.2 constraint block, storage balance with evaporation, the capacity band, the discharge band, nor the interval satisfaction functions that close the chapter, carries a name. Structure worth copying: this is the cleanest multi-objective skeleton in the sample. Three objectives, each one line with its justification above it; four constraints named in words before they are written as inequalities; a parameter section that closes every undefined symbol in turn; and only then the joint operation model with its own objective and its own constraints. It also does the thing almost no A paper does, defining dead water level and flood limited water level on the page, so the inequalities can be read by someone who does not already know dam engineering. Three verified defects. First, the safety constraint changes side mid-chapter: 5.1.1 writes Safety_sd >= Safety_Bd, safety being the quantity to be preserved, and 5.1.2 resolves safety into a risk loss index R = P N and then writes the system sum of R_i^sd <= P(K) N(K), so expanding the same symbol reverses the inequality and an implementer has to guess which side is meant. Second, the water benefit reads Is = sum over i sum over i of (S_ij - D_ij): the inner index repeats i, so the double sum collapses and the time index j drops out of the objective the dispatch model maximises. Third, each dam's risk index already contains its own cascade term, P(l|j) P(j) N(l) summed over downstream dams, and the system index then sums those indices over j, so a failure that takes two dams losses is charged once per upstream dam in the chain and the paper never says whether that double counting is intended. Smaller: 'We let [V_fi, V_Fi] to be the of V_it' has lost its predicate exactly where the interval relaxation is introduced.

note: Twenty-sixth type-A model chapter, chapter 4, file pages 6 to 13, printed pages 5 to 12, and the first artifact in a long run whose word count is right: twelve stored paragraphs and 2,300 claimed words against 2,358 raw words on those pages, about 2,294 without the running header. The names are section-anchored, one per paragraph, and say what the paragraph does: a named section, then a sentence such as use a geometry visual to motivate a standard capacity formula before simplification. Coded by the names, the chapter holds eighteen blocks rather than twelve, because the prerequisite list, the two observations on Figure 4 and the weighted restatement of the program are each a paragraph in their own right. Two defects in the artifact rather than the paper. Its sentence_words, rhetorical_proportions, move_types and counting_method fields are one identical tuple across all sixteen chapters, minimum 5 words, median 23, maximum 61, so those four fields are template values and cannot be quoted per chapter; only paragraph_count and word_count vary and only those were used here. And the chapter is coded at four different grains, a whole section in one name for 4.3, one paragraph per name for 4.1 to 4.2 and for 4.3.2. The chapter itself is a modular build to copy when the answer is a composite index: three sub-models, each with its own scope sentence, each reduced to one scored line, a declared sign for each score, then one nonlinear program whose objective is the weighted sum and whose constraints are capacity, dam count and position. The habit worth keeping is the two observations on Figure 4, each followed by a mechanism sentence, which is how a chapter reads its own curve instead of pointing at it. Five verified defects. First, the head in the power term is not the dam height: section 4.3.4 writes Supply = eta rho g h Q with h the dam height, Table 1 gives h as the height of dam i, and the expanded Final Value on page 12 replaces h(Xi) by L k(Xi), river length times bed slope, which is the fall over the whole river; the appendix code computes Power with k*l, so the substitution is the model and not a typo. Second, series safety has its sign backwards: the prose says the more evenly the dams are spaced the safer the system, formula (6) is a modified Pearson statistic whose numerator is a sum of squared deviations from the mean spacing, and section 4.3.5 then calls Series positively related to safety, while no reciprocal or minus sign appears in (6) as printed; the denominator of (6) does not survive the text layer, so I record a sign inconsistency to check rather than arithmetic to correct. Third, the risk objective adds money to a flow rate: fundamental investment is currency, risk loss is collapse probability times an index times a volumetric flow rate, and Risk is their sum, so the per-dam score is dimensionally incoherent before any normalization is applied, and the normalization cannot repair it. Fourth, the normalization described and the normalization used are different functions: 4.3.5 prints the min-max rescaling (x - min)/(max - min) to [0, 1] and then the model multiplies two features by (n-1)/L and inverts the third as min(Risk)/Risk, which is not min-max and does not bound anything to [0, 1]; page 12 adds that Supply and Series are scaled into [-1, 0] and writes no formula that does so. Fifth, the chapter says in one sentence that the goal is to minimize Final Value and writes max Final Value in the program two paragraphs later. Smaller, all verified: the acceptable-risk exponent 1.1 is said to be set by experiment and no experiment in the paper fits it, the string 1.1 appearing only inside formula (4) and in the derivative condition that follows it; prerequisite 4.3.1 says we replace Q(Xi;t) with Q(Xi;t), a symbol replaced by itself where the annual average was meant; eta carries two meanings, the extreme condition ratio of (5) and the turbine efficiency of (7); d carries two meanings, the river width of (2) and (3) and the mean spacing of (6); and five symbols enter the equations without a row in Table 1, the safety factor, the volume-to-expense coefficient, the cost constant lambda, and rho and g.

note: Twenty-seventh type-A model chapter, chapter 5, file pages 8 to 17, printed pages 5 to 14, the third 2017 A paper on the Kariba replacement and the only one of the three that builds the river as a field before it places anything. Word count again accurate: 2,875 claimed against 3,007 raw and 2,937 without the running header. The names are section-anchored and functional, but they are one per section, so 5.1.4, two pages of data acquisition, parameter values and eight figures, carries no name at all, and coded by paragraph the chapter runs to twenty-four blocks against thirteen names. Two artifact facts belong in the record. First, its per-chapter sentence_words, rhetorical_proportions and move_types are one identical tuple across all sixteen chapters, exactly as in P-A-2017-55280, so these two 2017 A artifacts come from one generator and only paragraph_count and word_count vary between them. Second, its chapter spans overlap: model-establishment 8 to 17, data-preprocessing 10 to 28, algorithm 10 to 22, results 11 to 24, model-improvement 14 to 22, so four chapters claim pages that are inside the model chapter and no per-chapter word count in this artifact can be disjoint; I measured the model chapter on the pages rather than trusting the span. What to copy: the derivation order is the cleanest in the A sample for a continuum model. A control volume named with its two ends, the balance written as words first, every term then expanded separately with its own identity, the expanded terms divided to leave a PDE, the same three steps repeated for energy with a constitutive law inserted in the middle rather than assumed at the start, then boundary data distinguished from initial state and both attributed to a measurement source. Then, honestly, the model is abandoned: 5.3 says the PDE system cannot absorb eleven dams in a bearable time and replaces it with a reach-by-reach recurrence, which is the transition most A papers make silently. Eight verified defects. First, the two sides of (16) do not carry the same dimensions: the left side holds rho g h y', a pressure per metre of length, added to k h, a velocity squared, while the right side holds h v dv/dx and h dv/dt and one half (q - phi) v, all squared velocities; the density is applied to one side only and the resistance term cannot be added to the gravity term at all. Second, the printed unit of k cannot satisfy either equation it enters: with k = 1.0e-6 kg m-3 s-1, (13) yields kg squared per square metre per second where a joule is required, and the coefficient that makes (13) a work is an acceleration, metres per second squared; no Manning n, Chezy C or friction slope is cited anywhere, so the only resistance constant in the model is unverifiable in its own units. Third, the expansion in (11) loses the factor two: the change of kinetic energy is written with v squared times the total differential of v where v times the differential of v squared, which is twice that, was meant. Fourth, (14) and (15) omit the channel width L that the rainfall and evaporation influxes carry in (3) and (4), so those two energy terms are energies per metre of reach and cannot be added to (11). Fifth, the initial state contradicts the model: (18) sets the velocity by free fall from the source, sqrt(v0 squared plus 2 g (y0 - y(x))), which is the solution with no resistance, in a chapter whose energy equation keeps a resistance term, and over a kilometre of fall that initial field reaches speeds no river carries. Sixth, the recurrence (32) is dimensionally wrong at its first term: one half g L l is a volume per second squared where the root must be a volume per second, and the same mismatch runs through the discriminant. Seventh, grey relation is applied to raw data: the weights come from correlation coefficients that live in zero to one, and Step 7 multiplies them by the raw x_i(j) with no normalization step printed, so the site score is dominated by whichever index carries the largest numbers, the width in metres, while the topographic indexes are 0 or 1. Eighth, the direction of one index contradicts the paragraph that motivates it: 5.2.1 calls a large current acceleration a hazard to transport and residents, and Step 1 takes the largest value of every metric as the reference ideal with the river width the only inversion, so acceleration is scored as if more of it were better. Smaller: g is printed as 9.8 m/s rather than m/s squared; the third column of Table 2 is headed A, the outflow coefficient of (30) and (31), carries degree values 33, 27, 16 and 11, and is then glossed as the relative gate opening, a fraction the next paragraph fixes at 0.25, 0.5 or 1.0; and 5.3.2 treats the reservoir area S_i as constant with depth.

note: Twenty-eighth type-A model chapter, and not a chapter at all in the ordinary sense: file pages 6 to 20, printed 5 to 19, hold sections 4.1 through 10, so this label covers the whole modelling body, potential cost, fuzzy benefit scoring, ROI, the water balance, the three capacities, siting, flow regulation, sensitivity and the Monte Carlo risk, and the span begins mid-sentence inside 4.1. Nineteen names, one per formula cluster, and they are the most useful names of the three 2017 Kariba papers because each one states the modelling act rather than the topic: write reservoir storage as prior storage plus inflow minus release, loss and external use; bound the reservoir state and separate normal maximum from flood-reserve maximum; expose a separate downstream discharge limit after the storage constraint. Coded by paragraph the span runs to twenty-six blocks, eight of them blocks no name covers: the search over subsets with its flowchart, the fourteen chosen dams, the 2008 error analysis, the normal-year allocation table, the drought and flood allocation tables. Two artifact faults. Its per-chapter sentence_words, rhetorical_proportions and move_types are again the one identical tuple, the third 2017 A artifact from that generator. And its spans overlap so badly that no word count can be checked: pages 6 to 20 measure 5,166 prose words against 2,260 claimed, because results 6 to 21, algorithm 12 to 30, data-preprocessing 5 to 35 and sensitivity 19 to 20 all claim pages inside the model span, and the artifact's own ambiguity note admits counts follow rhetorical ownership rather than page area; I therefore record no density figure for this paper. Six verified defects, all by arithmetic on the paper's own numbers. The benefit score contradicts its own membership vector: the text says the grades are 0.48, 0.56 and 0.515 and builds the benefit column on 0.64, the third option's second component, so 0.515 appears nowhere and the table is right where the sentence is wrong. The fuzzy weights 0.2, 0.25, 0.35 and 0.2 are published with no derivation, and the four-by-five membership matrices that would produce the three printed vectors are never printed, so neither the weights nor the grades can be checked. The cardinality programme is decorative: (19) minimizes the count of dams while (20) requires the count between ten and twenty, so the optimum is pinned at its own lower bound, and the answer of fourteen dams is produced by increasing the count in the search flowchart rather than by solving the programme, with nothing shown to establish that ten, eleven, twelve or thirteen dams fail the capacity constraint. The allocation table contradicts the advice drawn from it in the normal case: the text says storage should be raised in July through January, while Table 8 prints a negative change in October, November, December and January for all three subsystems and positives from February to June. The drought reading contradicts Table 9: subsystem 1 is said to be always discharging and subsystem 3 always impounding, while five of the twelve entries for subsystem 1 are negative and seven of the twelve for subsystem 3 are positive. And the error analysis explains its bias with a term the model already carries: ten of the twelve monthly estimates sit above the observation, and the residual is attributed to missing evaporation and infiltration, which are the internal loss term I(i,t) of the balance in (5). The one thing this chapter does better than the other two 2017 papers is the error check itself: twelve months of observed discharge against the model, absolute and fractional error per month, an average of 5.68 per cent that I verified against the table row by row.

note: Twenty-ninth type-A model chapter: file pages 5 to 19, printed 4 to 18, sections 3.1 to 6.3, a skywave link budget that is then rebuilt twice, once across the sea surface and once across dry, mountain and forest ground, with a ship-sway perturbation added at the end. Eighteen stored names, 33 equations, and ten numbered figures on the span against a recorded figure count of zero. The span closes inside 6.3 at (33): the last page opens the section whose heading promises a communication time and the record stops at the refraction integral, so the duration never appears inside the coded pages. Coded by paragraph the span runs to thirty-six blocks, about half of them unnamed: the scenario page, the simulated loss and the received power, the readings of Figure 2 and Figure 3, the evaluation of the roughness factor at fifteen metres per second, the two reflected powers and their ratio, the SNR arithmetic, the smooth-terrain value, the substitution page that separates the three-hop answer from the two-hop one, and the four numbered findings taken off Figure 7. Four numbers in this chapter are exactly right and I recomputed all four: the roughness correction, with g = h sin(theta)/lambda = 0.0541 giving 0.8044 against the printed 0.8043; the wave height 0.0051 v squared at fifteen metres per second giving 1.1475; the PM spectrum (13) in its standard form; and the 9.1133 dB smooth-terrain reflection loss, which is exactly the circular-polarization average of the Fresnel powers for a relative permittivity of four at 45 degrees, 0.20378 and 0.04152 averaging to 0.12265, that is minus 9.1133 dB. Verified defects, all arithmetic on the paper numbers. The loss chain cannot hold: 100 W through 97.4597 dB leaves 1.79e-5 mW, not the printed 0.43248 mW, which itself implies 53.64 dB, and the 0.2832 mW carried into the hop count implies 55.48 dB, so three printed values disagree about the same link. And 97.4597 dB is below the free-space term alone: (2) at the paper own effective path of 200 times root two km and 20 MHz gives 107.49 dB, and (3) to (5) at the paper own parameters, R = 110, noon on 1 July, 26 degrees north, add 4.97 dB, so the model as written returns 112.46 dB and the printed total is 15 dB under its own model and 10 dB under free space, which no positive absorption term can produce. The CCIR fits never run: (9) returns 70 for f at or below 2253.5895 MHz and (10) returns 5.0 for f at or below 1106.207 MHz, so at the working frequency of 20 MHz both are read off their constants and the published five-term and six-term polynomials do no work, so both fits are decorative at the only frequency the paper ever uses. The smooth-sea reflected power exceeds the incident power: P1 is 0.4378 mW against an incident 0.43248 mW, a ratio of 1.0123, while the paper own circular average of the Fresnel powers for 70 minus 4500i at 45 degrees is 0.95605, giving 0.4135 mW, so the printed value is 5.9 per cent high and a passive surface cannot return more than it receives. The two formulas the argument needs are missing: (18) and (19) are blanks on page 12 where the circular-polarization average and the rough-to-smooth ratio belong, and no page quotes (20). The foliage coefficient contradicts its stated range: 0.01 to 0.1 dB per metre is given for the 3 to 30 MHz band and 0.8 is substituted over ten metres, eight times the upper bound, for 8 dB of foliage loss against the 0.1 to 1 dB the range allows, and that substitution sits on the margin that separates the three-hop smooth answer from the two-hop mountain one. The SNR formula does follow from its two parents but with the frequency sign flipped: 201.56 is exactly 137.2 plus 96.8 minus 32.44, so substituting (2) into the difference of (21) and (22) reproduces the constant, and the frequency term must then be plus 20 lg f, which (23) prints as minus 20 lg f, so the term is out by 52.04 dB at 20 MHz, twice 20 lg 20, with the antenna gain Gt of (21) silently dropped. The receiver bandwidth is given in decibels, 6 dB in a term that already carries 10 lg B. Equation (3) is printed with the free-space symbol L_bf over the ionospheric absorption it is introduced to define. Three ship motions are listed as a six-degree-of-freedom model. A sentence about wind speed and wave height is printed twice verbatim on page 10. The page that repeats the propagation-model sentence points at Figure 8 while its own caption is Figure 9. The four numbered findings read off Figure 7 are two claims each stated twice, once as distance and once as loss, and no plotted value is printed. The footer breaks twice, page 14 of the file printing Page 12 of 22 between neighbours that say of 24, and pages 16 and 17 both printing Page 16 of 24. No word density is recorded: 4,180 words on pages 5 to 19 against 2,490 claimed, with seven other chapter spans lying inside the same pages.

note: Thirtieth type-A record, and the widest span so far: file pages 4 to 14, printed 3 to 13, beginning mid-sentence inside the Introduction subsection C, Our Model, and then carrying the whole of II Background, A transmitter and receiver, B radio propagation and loss, C skywave channel interaction, D performance evaluation, the whole of III Assumptions, the Nomenclature table, all of IV Model Development, A construction with its three subsections and B validation, and it stops on the last page as V Model Application opens. Because the span carries background and assumptions, its profile of fifteen define blocks out of twenty-nine is inflated by construction and this record should be read as the paper's whole front half rather than as a model chapter. Twelve stored names, and they are the fourth naming family in this ledger: every one begins with the identical prefix, 'Use this ordered move to make Model Construction auditable:', and the only content is the four-stage arrow chain after it, so the names describe the computation rather than the topic and are more useful than any stub family before, but they also guarantee that twelve names cover twelve moves of one kind and never mark a figure, a source choice or a result. Two of the twelve do not resolve. Name 7, path-dependent electron density and collisions into non-deviative absorption, has no paragraph anywhere in the paper: the only occurrences of absorption after the background pages are the symbol k in the nomenclature table and the term L_absorption inside (22). Name 8, great-circle distance and bearing into a landing position, has no paragraph inside the span, and the bearing and position material sits on page 15 in the scenario setup and again in the memo. Both are recorded unresolved rather than guessed. Five numbers in the chapter are right and I checked each: 100 W is 50 dBm as printed; the budget is 180.06 dB deep and the remaining allowance to hold a 10 dB margin over a -120 dBm floor is 170.06, which is the printed 180 and 170; the phase dispersion 4 pi dh sin(theta)/lambda is the Rayleigh form; the complex term gamma = 18e9 sigma / f is the 60 lambda sigma imaginary part written for f in hertz, giving 30,000 for sea water at 3 MHz; and the reflection law (20) with its cosine (21) is the vector form of equal angles. Verified defects. The two loss terms the budget rests on are never written: L_free and L_absorption enter (22) and the hop count depends on them, while the only term with an equation behind it is the terrain term, so a chapter that derives a Fresnel coefficient to the third decimal leaves the free-space and absorption debits as words. The quantitative validation is a restatement of the background: pages 6 and 14 give the same 2500 to 5000 km hop range, and the second is offered as the model's result. Two scale faults on the terrain patch: the ten by ten metre mesh cannot carry the fifteen metre swell the same paper imposes as the super-turbulent sea, and the fifty by fifty sample of one-arcsecond SRTM data spans about 1.5 km, so rescaling it to ten metres compresses the horizontal scale about 151 times, which means a 45 degree facet in the model would need 1.5 km of relief in the source data. Two artefacts of bookkeeping: the NASA epoch is 1 January 2001 at 1:30 GMT on page 10 and 1 January 2000 on page 14, and the nomenclature gives A in km and B in m, two path lengths in two units in one table. And the assumption that a mountainous region has sharp deviations in the tens of metres is followed, eight pages later, by a mesh whose elevation changes are smoothed to ten metres or less. No density figure is recorded: pages 4 to 14 hold 3,855 words against 984 claimed, because the claimed count is the sum of the twelve named moves and because problem-analysis, data-preprocessing, algorithm, robustness and results spans all overlap these pages.

note: Thirty-first type-A record and the worst naming in the ledger. The fifteen stored names are three themes crossed with five rhetorical forms: screen inadmissible cases, extend a transparent baseline through a correction interface, expose shared structure while isolating the parameters that change across media, each repeated verbatim for the paragraph-chain form, the compact-sentence form, the evidence-bridge form, the handoff-transition form and the boundary-check form. Not one word of the fifteen refers to this paper, its ionosphere, its sea surface or its terrain, so the field holds a template grid rather than names; the chapter was coded from the pages and the record carries the placeholder flag. The span is file pages 6 to 16, printed 5 to 14: the tail of the assumption list, the notation table, 3.1 model description, 3.2 the ionosphere in five subsections from the D-layer attenuation through the refractive index, the E layer, the F layer with its micro-element recursion and the MUF, 3.3 the sea, 3.4 the ground, 3.5 free-space path loss and 3.6 background noise, and it stops on the noise figure as 4 Result begins. Six things in it are right and I checked each: the wavelength to frequency correspondence, 20, 17 and 15 m against 15, 17.65 and 20 MHz; the imaginary coefficient 300 lambda, which is 60 lambda sigma with sigma at 5 S/m, giving 4,500 at 15 m; the resistivity to conductivity inversion, 10 to 100 ohm metres becoming 0.01 to 0.1 siemens per metre with the midpoint 0.05 taken; the 32.45 constant of (13) for kilometres and megahertz; the critical condition that reflection begins when the ray angle reaches 90 degrees; and the choice of horizontal polarization, which is the flatter of the two coefficients against grazing angle and is shown to be so in both Figure 5 and Figure 7. Verified defects. The advice in 3.4 contradicts its own sentence: the paragraph reads the reduction factor as falling when the grazing angle rises, which makes small grazing angles the good ones, then says that electromagnetic waves with a small incident angle are the ones likely to lose energy, and then recommends the small grazing angle, so incidence and grazing are collapsed into one phrase and the middle sentence is wrong as printed. The ground is a building material: relative permittivity 15 from a range given for wet concrete and conductivity 0.05 from a range given for concrete, with no statement of what terrain the problem's ground is meant to be, so the dry-mountain case of the question is answered with a wall. The physical unit is printed with an equals sign where the division belongs, dB=km for the D-layer coefficient and m=s and 10-100 m for metres per second and ohm metres in 3.4, and the figure caption repeats it. And the span ends without a budget: the D-layer attenuation, the surface reflection, the free-space loss and the background noise are each derived in turn and nothing joins the four into a received power inside these pages. One cross-paper check rather than a defect: the imaginary part of the permittivity is printed here as 70 plus i300 lambda and in P-A-2018-76082 as 70 minus 4,500i, the same 60 lambda sigma term at 15 m, so the two cannot both match their own Fresnel forms, but the extraction drops signs in several places and I record this as a sign to check, not as arithmetic to correct. No density figure is recorded: 2,320 words on those pages against 552 claimed, with four other spans overlapping them.

note: Thirty-second type-A record. The thirty-six stored names are nine themes crossed with four rhetorical forms, the paragraph-chain, compact-sentence, evidence-handoff and boundary-check forms, so the field is a template grid again and the chapter was coded from the pages; unlike P-A-2018-77845 the nine themes are this paper's own moves, wave complexity to a computable surrogate, three-dimensional extension, geometric upper bound, dominant-loss triage, baseline then correction, correction composition, signal-noise gate, cross-medium analogy and static-model boundary, and each theme carries a page and a real source excerpt, but nine phrases still cannot name thirty-four blocks. Span is file pages 7 to 21, printed 4 to 18: the notation table, 4.1 HF propagation and the ionosphere and the usable frequency, 4.2 the Longuet-Higgins, spectral and three-dimensional wave models with the simulation figure, 4.3 the four-part budget, free-space loss and the one-jump bound, absorption with the index that is then dropped for a constant, calm and turbulent sea reflection with the two correction factors, the additional loss, the first reflection intensity, field strength, noise and SNR, the hop scaling, 5 the ground comparison, 6.1 the moving-receiver time budget, 6.2 the frequency table, and it stops inside 7 Strengths. Eight things are right and I checked each: the band correspondence, 3 to 30 MHz against 100 to 10 m; the 0.85 MUF operating point; the wind reference 19.5 m of the PM spectrum; the 234.0 that (22) builds from 137.2 plus 96.8 and then reduces to 201.56 by taking 32.44 out of the free-space term; the cancellation of 20 lg f between (20) and (21), which leaves the frequency dependence of (22) coming only from the path-loss term, 23.52 dB at 15 MHz; the one-jump bound itself, which with 6371 km, a 3 degree minimum elevation and a 300 km virtual height gives 3224.5 km, exactly the r the table uses for one hop; the hop arithmetic, 3225 doubled to 6450 printed as 6449 and tripled to 9675 printed as 9674; and the 3000 km refit step, which is that same 3225 km rounded. Verified defects. (5) prints Li while the notation table and every heading say La, so the budget names a symbol that is never defined. (19) describes P1 as the transmitting power and P0 as the first reflection intensity, which reverses both the notation table and Table 1, where P0 is the 100 W transmitter. The one-jump bound is stated as 4000 km for F2 and then contradicted by the paper's own table, which uses the 3225 km the formula actually gives, so the text and the numbers come from two different virtual heights with no reconciliation. Table 1 sets the working frequency to 100 MHz for a paper whose own band is 3 to 30 MHz, and Table 4 is headed f = 15 Hz where the text says 15 MHz. The four printed SNR rows cannot come from one set of parameters: with (22) and (23) to (25), differencing consecutive rows implies a reflection loss of about 20.8 dB between one hop and two, then minus 1.2 dB between two and three, then 2.6 dB between three and four, and the two unknowns that would absorb a constant, the noise bandwidth and the atmospheric noise figure, cancel in the differences; and 20.8 dB is impossible for this paper's own reflection model, because both correction factors are fractions and the calm coefficient cannot exceed one, so a first-hop loss that large needs a product of correction factors near 0.0083, which no figure in the paper shows. That same implied loss also contradicts the comparison in 5, where flat ground at 6.53 dB is presented as the worse surface and still reaches four hops against the sea's six. The absorption index (9) is derived from a sunspot number and a zenith angle that are never given a value, and is then replaced by a constant 4 dB, so the formula is decorative at the only place it could be used. The equation numbering is not a count: 24 is printed twice, for the hop-scaled reflection loss and again for the SNR threshold, and 26 is never printed at all. The bandwidth is labelled in dB inside a 10 lg term, the same unit error as in P-A-2018-76082. The antenna gain of (20) disappears from (22) with no statement that it is taken as unity. The power unit is ambiguous by 30 dB, since (20) asks for kilowatts and Table 1 hands it 100 W. The six hops returned by fsolve arrive with no stated target, while (24) does state one, SNR at or above 10 dB, and by Table 4 that boundary is reached at four hops over 10,125 km, with five and six only at shorter ranges, so the six is a stopping choice and not a computed maximum. In 5 the text takes relative permittivity 3 to 8 as the basic value and Table 3 then lists wet soil at 10 to 30, so the stated range matches only the dry-soil row, and Table 3's permittivity column is headed in farads per metre while holding values that are plainly relative. In the wave model the random initial phase is drawn between 0 and a quarter period, which biases the superposition instead of randomizing it. And the absolute level of every SNR cannot be checked at all: the noise bandwidth and the atmospheric noise figure are never printed, and Table 2 is an image of the CCIR data with no single value quoted in the text. No density figure: 3,645 words on those pages against 396 claimed, with six other spans overlapping them.

note: Thirty-third type-A record, and the purest instruction-template naming in the ledger. The fifteen stored names are five move labels crossed with three rhetorical forms, paragraph-chain, sentence-frame and handoff-boundary, and the function body in every one of them is the same boilerplate sentence, expand the complete observable paragraph progression for the action of something while preserving some boundary, so only the slot label names anything at all; but the five slots are real landmarks, 4.1 opening, Rate closure, Equations 2-4, Figure 1 interpretation and Weight-to-energy handoff, and the chapter was coded from the pages with the record flagged. Span is file pages 5 to 7, printed 4 to 6: the notation table, 4.1 the logistic weight model from the observation that growth decelerates through (1), the initial value problem (2), its closed form (3), the three data points and the fitted (4) with Figure 1 and the reading that puts maturity at eight years, then 4.2.1 Kleiber's law, the human metabolic formula (5), the 80 kg man and the 2,751 kcal reference, the ratio (6) and the substituted curve (7), and it stops as 4.2.2 opens. Five things are right: (3) is the exact solution of (2); (5) returns 1,926 kcal a day for 80 kg, 180 cm and 20 years with the standard men's coefficients, 13.7, 5, minus 6.8 and 66; the division by 0.7 gives 2,751.4, printed as 2,751; (6) applies the three-quarter exponent to the mass ratio and not to the mass; and (4) at age three returns 14,003.8 kg, which is the 14,000 kg datum. Verified defects, and this is the worst arithmetic in the A sample. (4) does not pass through the second datum: evaluated at one year it returns 112.45 kg against the stated 35 kg, so the printed curve fits birth and age three and ignores the middle point. The three points cannot be fit by this model at all: with a birth mass of 10 kg, a logistic through 35 kg at one year and 14,000 kg at three years has no solution, and the weight at age three cannot exceed about 429 kg however large the asymptote is made, so the calibration is impossible rather than merely inaccurate. The asymptote is 1,481,000 kg, one thousand four hundred and eighty-one tonnes, against the 14 tonnes the paper calls the adult dragon, and because the figure's vertical axis is labelled in units of one hundred thousand kilograms the plot reads as a curve topping out at 14.8; the text then reads that asymptote as the dragon reaching its maximum weight at eight years and calls the animal mature there. (7) is not (6) with the paper's own reference mass: at age zero (6) forces the dragon to consume exactly 2,751 kcal a day, and (7) returns 646, so the printed constant is 4.26 times too small and is exactly what (6) gives with a reference mass near 69 kg rather than the 10 kg birth mass. (5) also reuses w0 for the man's weight, a symbol the notation table assigns to the dragon's birth mass, and introduces h0 and a0 that the table does not list. And the formula is attributed to the American Sports Medicine Association when it is the Mifflin-St Jeor equation for men. Two smaller ones: (1) prints r where the surrounding text and (2) use r0, and 4.2.2 opens by referring to the calorie consumption at one year old, which 4.2.1 never evaluates. No density figure: 1,091 words on those pages against 243 claimed, with six other spans overlapping them.

note: Thirty-fourth type-A record, the second dragon paper of 2019 and the second instruction-template naming. The eighteen stored names are six move labels crossed with three rhetorical forms, expand the progression for something, compress it to one source-bounded sentence frame, preserve the transition and terminal boundary, and each body is a fixed sentence with a variable slot, so only the slot names anything; the slots are real landmarks, Balerion scaling, the two-analogue estimate, growth data selection, model selection, the length-to-mass modification and the fitted curve, and the chapter was coded from the pages with the record flagged. Span is file and printed pages 4 to 7: 3.3 the case for indeterminate growth, 3.3.1 sizing Balerion by scaling a crocodile by its teeth and then bracketing a pterosaur against a komodo dragon, 3.3.2 the candidate growth families and the choice, 3.3.3 the von Bertalanffy form carried to weight, the parameter list, the anchors and the rejection of the problem's given weights, the episode sizes, the fitted curve, and 3.4 the metabolic rate from a human to an elephant to a blue whale with the cow count, and it stops on Balerion's daily requirement. Nine numbers are right and I checked each: one watt per kilogram as 20.65 kcal per kilogram a day, which is 86,400 joules over 4,184; 65.3 as 20.65 times the fourth root of 100; the elephant at 8.82 kcal per kilogram; the daily need as rate times mass, 65.3 times W to the three quarters; Balerion at 663,107 kcal and 1.33 cows; 979.7 kW for 40.46 cows; the whale at 8.7 kcal per kilogram and the 177.4 rebasing; 3.6 cows on the whale-based law; and the fitted curve itself, which returns 5.02 kg at birth, 29.77 kg at one year, 219,901 kg at 220 years and 2,238 kg at nine years, giving 21,249 kcal a day against the printed 21,247. Verified defects. The pterosaur estimate is a factor of ten out: 250 kg scaled by the cube of 150 over 9 is 1,157,407 kg, printed as 115,740. The komodo estimate silently uses the fifty metre length that the crocodile scaling produced, after the paragraph above has fixed Balerion at forty-two metres; at forty-two metres the same law gives 192,080 kg, and the printed 324,074 is exactly 70 times the cube of fifty over three. The average of the two printed weights is 219,907, printed as 219,901, and that figure then becomes the anchor of every fit in the paper. The model choice contradicts the requirement it states: the section argues the dragons grow without limit and so there should be no asymptote, then adopts the one equation it has just called bounded, and the resolution it offers, early exponential growth, does not remove the bound; the fitted bound is 223,348 kg, 1.6 percent above Balerion, so the chosen model's ceiling is the largest known dragon's own weight and the premise does no work. The no-limit alternative is stated with the condition that any y with a second derivative below one qualifies, which is dimensionally meaningless and is not the condition for attenuating growth. The metabolic conversion is halved: the range 0.3 to 9 watts per kilogram is written as 3 to 92 kcal per kilogram against the paper's own 20.65 kcal per watt per kilogram, so the correct range is 6.2 to 186 and the cow bracket of 1.32 to 40.46 should be about 2.7 to 83. The fitted curve is written in x where the model is parameterised in t. And the assumption that dragons live about 250 years is justified by a dragon that lived to 220 and then never used, because every fit anchors on 220. No density figure: 1,539 words on those pages against 665 claimed, with six other spans overlapping them.

note: Thirty-fifth type-A record, the third instruction-template naming in a row and the largest stored list of the three. The thirty-three stored names are eleven move labels crossed with three rhetorical forms, and every body is a fixed sentence around a slot, so only the slot names anything; the slots come straight from the section numbering, Section 3 opening, Figure 1, 3.1, 3.1.1, 3.1.2, Equation 2-3, Figure 2, 3.1.3, 3.2, 3.3, Equation 7-8, and the chapter was coded from the pages with the record flagged. Span is file pages 5 to 9, printed 2 to 6: the end of the assumption list, the symbol table, Section 3 and its framework figure, 3.1 energy expenditure with Kleiber's law, the rest and action split, the four flying animals, the log-linear fit and the two constants, 3.1.3 the fire-breathing mechanism and its roasting energy, 3.2 the food chain with the assimilation rate, 3.3 the energy budget with (5) to (8), and 3.4.1 opens the size bound with the bone table before the span ends on the stress formula. Four things are right and I checked each: the two constants are the exponentials of the printed intercepts, 36.6 and 270.4, and both then reproduce all eight table values to within about a fifth, with the rest line low by five percent at the smallest bird and high by eleven at the largest; the slope of minus 0.25 is exactly the b minus one of the same section, so the fit and the law agree by construction; (6) is algebraically what it claims, assimilated minus fire equals intake times a constant; and (7) and (8) differentiate (5) and (6) consistently, with the expenditure rate of (4) entering unchanged. Verified defects. Table 3 breaks its own rule: the text says the assimilation rate can be had from respiration, which makes it 60 to 70 percent, 40 to 50 and 5 to 10 for the three classes, and the table prints 60 to 70, 70 to 80 and 90 to 95, so two of its three rows contradict the method that produced the column and the dragon's 90 percent is taken from a row that cannot be derived that way. The coefficient K of (6) to (8) is the whole point of folding the fire cost into the energy budget and is never evaluated, although the paper's own two constants make it 0.5655. The fire constant 6.69 million joules per kilogram of food is labelled estimation with no calculation behind it, against an intake of 20 million joules per kilogram in the same pages, so a third of the assimilated energy goes to roasting. And the last coded page defines the stress formula without its number, which the next page then cites as equation (9). No density figure: 1,905 words on those pages against 614 claimed, with three other spans overlapping them.
