note: Thirty-sixth type-A record and the fourth instruction-template naming in a row, the smallest of the four at five moves crossed with three forms. Each body is one fixed sentence around a slot, so only the slot names anything, and the five slots are the subsection's own moves: logistic family selection, uncertainty-aware parameter claim, time-to-state derivative conversion, environment-ready growth interface, finite-rate slowdown explanation. The artifact's chapter span is wrong and the record is coded from the pages: it allots model-establishment one physical page, file 7, with 139 words and five paragraphs, but the table of contents puts 3.1 on printed 4 and 3.2 on printed 6, so the section runs from the bottom of printed page 4 to the top of printed page 6, and the one page it does claim also carries the start of 3.2 and 3.3, so the 139 words are the subsection's move labels and not its prose. Span coded is section 3.1 entire, file pages 5 to 7: the goal and the problem quote, Table 1, the maximal-growth assumption, the wingspan-to-height conversion, the cube law m = a h cubed with a = 0.01134408, Balerion picked from lore, Figure 2 with Aegon at 6 ft 4 in, the 10:1 length to height ratio and 76 m, the length-cube ratio to 6,000,000 kg, the observation that a hundred years changed nothing so growth must slow, the choice of a sigmoidal curve, (1), the chi-squared fit with L = 843.717523 and k = 0.71173635, the derivative, and the change of variables to (2). Two things are right and I checked each: (2) is the exact derivative of m = a h cubed through the logistic, 3 m k (1 - (m / (a L cubed)) to the one third) with the 1/365 converting a per-year rate to a per-day one, so the algebra and the unit conversion both hold; and the wingspan-to-height factor is used consistently, 2520.5 over 3.75 giving 672 in at six years and 240 over 3.75 giving 64 in at eighteen months. Verified defects. The fitted pair (L, k) does not fit the data it is said to have been fitted to: with t0 solved from the birth point the curve gives 19.1 in at one year against a measured 16, 27.0 at eighteen months against 64 and 378.8 at six years against 672, and with t0 solved from the six-year point it gives 43.8 in at birth against 9.5, 84.6 at one year against 16 and 115.8 at eighteen months against 64; the best single t0 for the printed pair mispredicts birth by a factor of 3.5 and one year by a factor of 4.2. t0 itself is never printed anywhere in the paper, so (1) as written cannot be evaluated by a reader and every downstream number rests on a curve the paper does not specify. The chi-squared test the names call uncertainty-aware is never shown: no residuals, no statistic, no standard errors on L or k, and no statement of which of the four table points entered the fit. The cube law with a fitted at the hatchling explodes: 9.5 in gives 9.7 kg, matching the 10 kg in the table, but the same a gives 46.5 kg at the one-year height of 16 in against the table's 35, 2,974 kg at eighteen months and 3,442,525 kg at six years, so the calibration reproduces the birth mass alone and then puts a six-year-old dragon at three and a half thousand tonnes. The two length statements in the same paragraph cannot both hold: the 10:1 ratio applied to Drogon's own 672 in height gives 171 m, while the paper calls Drogon 61 m long, and the Balerion figure of 76 m is that same ratio applied to a 304 in height, so the rule that produces Balerion contradicts the length the paper gives for Drogon, and the 6,000,000 kg for Balerion is the length-cube ratio (76/61) cubed times Drogon's 3.44 million kg, which is 6.66 million, roughly right as a ratio but built on a mass three orders above any animal. The logistic asymptote, a L cubed, is 6.81 million kg, 13.6 percent above the 6.0 million the paper derives for Balerion, so even the curve's ceiling overshoots the largest dragon the paper sizes. No density figure: about 810 clean words on the span against 139 claimed, a factor of nearly six.

Only the move names anything: method-to-stochastic-traits rationale, nested object architecture, normalized habitat-factor construction, agent-state initialization, stochastic climate generator, resource-acquisition state transition, resource-gated settlement transition, allometry-to-integer prey demand, suitability-and-den movement rule, health-and-environment cost table, mate-conditional reproduction rule, fallback reproduction rule, daily survival reward update, fullness-binned mass transition. This is the agent-based half of the 2019 problem; the paper runs a differential equation model for one region beside it, and the artifact files only the ABM under model-establishment. Span is file pages 5 to 8, printed 2 to 5, section 4.2 entire: the motivation for an ABM, the 45-ecoregion map, the Earth object and dragon placement, region dryness, land and ice fractions, Table 1, the prey calorie mechanics and the suitability index, dragon initialisation, the globe timestep, the seasonal temperature generator and its figure, then the dragon's five phases with Table 2 between them, and the daily reward and fullness transitions. Correct and checked: the temperature generator is internally consistent, since 4S - 4(4 - C) is the same as 4(S - 4 + C) that the text names, and with S at its maximum of 4 and C at 2 the two draws give at most 16 + 2 times 4 times 4.25, exactly the 50 C ceiling the paragraph claims, reached in the tropical summer as stated; and the predation law's unit chain holds, a per-year energy law divided by 365 and then by 5000 kcal per prey unit, with the ceiling function making the answer an integer count of prey items, which is what the calorie rating 0 to 10 requires. Verified defects. Table 1 sets the arctic temperature to 0 and the suitability index divides the temperature by T, the maximum possible temperature of the region, so every arctic region carries a division by zero and its suitability is undefined or infinite, which is the opposite of the paper's own conclusion that the arctic is the hostile case. Two temperature encodings sit two pages apart: Table 1 puts the tropics at 15 C and temperate at 5, while the generator maps climate to 0, 1 and 2 and returns anything between minus 8 and 50 for the tropics, so a tropical winter is colder than the temperate mean the table gives. Table 2 and the hunting paragraph disagree on what a kill costs the region, 10 forests per activity in the table and one forest per prey in the text, a factor of ten over the same event. The forest level is written as (land - ice) over (1 + dryness) with no maximum, and the suitability index divides it by F, so the normalisers are never stated; the index is also called a weighted sum while every weight in the printed mean is one fifth. The predation law never prints a or b, so the paper's central energetics cannot be evaluated from the text, and the ceiling makes one prey item of up to 5000 kcal the minimum daily intake for any dragon of any mass, up to fifty times a hatchling's need. Gold mining draws a uniform count of twenty centred on current health, so a healthy dragon mines about a hundred nuggets a day against a maximum regional stock of 500, which empties any region's gold in five days and makes the 50-nugget den threshold trivial; the mining rate is capped by the stock but never by work. And reproduction at 25 percent a day with fecundity borrowed from clutch-laying reptiles gives each mature dragon about ninety offspring a year while the paper argues the opposite way round, lowering clutch size and raising frequency without checking the product. Density figure is honest here: 1,833 raw words on the span against 1,804 claimed, so the artifact counted table cells and formula fragments but lost almost nothing.

note: Thirty-eighth type-A record, the sixth instruction-template naming in a row and the first of the 2020 problem, ten moves crossed with three forms, thirty stored names for seventeen located blocks. Only the move names anything: space-time field definition, per-grid differenced autoregression, expected-difference recursion, normal-error uncertainty premise, lag-design matrix estimation, normal-equation solution, six-fold RMSE comparison, per-cell coefficient implementation, recursive residual-field forecast, deterministic-versus-ensemble branch. Span is file pages 8 to 10, printed 5 to 7: the opening claim that temperature is driven by radiation, heat loss and biological exchange so a vector autoregression is wanted, 4.1 the longitude-latitude field, the 690 fishing points with sixty years each, the sixty-year spring plot, the choice of ARIMA(p, d, 0), (2) the differenced autoregression, the normal residual, (3) the recursive expectation, the normality premise, (4) the prediction with its innovation, the fifty-year spread argument, 4.3.1 the design matrix (5), the normal equations (6), the k-fold search, the RMSE grid and ARIMA(1, 1, 0), and 4.3.2's handoff to the predicted field. Correct and checked: (6) is the ordinary least-squares solution to the system in (5), and (3) is the exact recursive expectation of (2), so estimator and prediction recursion both follow. The lag choice is also internally consistent, a model with one lag and one difference being written ARIMA(1, 1, 0). Verified defects. The printed design matrix runs off its own sample: the last row's target is the difference at p plus sixty, which for any positive order is past the sixty observations the paragraph above says exist, where the last target available is the difference at sixty. The four symbols are the same letter: the innovation is epsilon, its variance is written epsilon squared at the same index, the predictive variance is sigma squared with no relation to either, and the difference order d multiplies the notation inconsistently, (2) and (3) carrying the d-th difference while (4) carries the first. (4) is only valid for a first difference, though the model is fitted over a grid that includes other orders, and it adds a draw of the innovation to the prediction, so the printed forecast is a random realisation and not a forecast. The model cannot produce the warming the paper goes on to predict: with the autoregressive coefficient inside the unit circle the recursive expectation (3) decays to zero, so the expected fifty-year field is the present field and only the added noise moves, which means any predicted migration comes from the ensemble draws rather than from the fitted dynamics, and the fitted dynamics were chosen after finding no trend in the data. The data are spring temperature only, as Figure 5's caption says, while the model is stated for the temperature of the point with no season subscript, so the paper's fifty-year field silently inherits one season. No density figure: 754 raw words on the span against 1,005 claimed, an overcount of a third, the mirror image of the previous paper's near-exact count.

note: Thirty-ninth type-A record, the seventh instruction-template naming in a row, ten moves crossed with three forms, thirty stored names for twenty-two located blocks. Only the move names anything: reference-sequence definition, comparison-sequence definition, grey relational coefficient, relation-grade aggregation, original-to-AGO state, whitened differential equation, least-squares parameter interface, time-response solution, inverse accumulation recovery, posterior error-ratio validation. Span is file pages 6 to 8, printed 5 to 7: 4.2.1 grey relational analysis with the reference and comparison sequences, the coefficient and its two-level minima, Table 2, then 4.2.2 the case for a grey system, the choice of GM(1, 1) said to be enhanced with the influencing factors, the original sequence for 1980 to 2020, the whitened equation, the least-squares pair, the mean-generating operator, the exponential time response, the inverse accumulation, the residual definition and the two variances, then 4.2.3 with 225 locations, Figure 2, Table 3 and the acceptance sentence. Correct and checked: the relational coefficient is the standard form with the two-level minimum, the two-level maximum and the resolution constant; the whitened equation, the design matrix with the mean-generated regressor and a unit column, the least-squares pair, the exponential time response and the inverse accumulation are all the textbook GM(1, 1) and are written correctly; and every residual in Table 3 is the printed actual minus the printed prediction to the fourth decimal, all eight of them. Verified defects. The paper's central acceptance claim is false on its own table: the c ratio, the dispersion of the residuals over the dispersion of the observations, computed from the eight printed rows, is 4.0 on standard deviations and 16.0 on variances, against the grey-model thresholds of 0.35 for excellent, 0.5 for good and 0.65 for qualified, so the model is rejected by its own test while the text calls the ratio small and calls the model acceptable. The residuals say the same thing one way: every one after 2005 is negative and they grow monotonically to minus 1.44, the prediction rises 0.236 degrees a year while the observations rise 0.0013, and the mean residual is minus 0.556, which is bias and not dispersion, so a dispersion criterion cannot see it. The announced enhancement never appears: GM(1, 1) is introduced as enhanced with the other influencing factors, the correlation table ranks greenhouse gas, forest cover and population, and none of the three enters the differential equation, the design matrix or the response. Table 2 also cannot be produced by its own sub-values: the human grade is printed as 0.9988 above sub-factors of 0.9784 and 0.9132, the environmental grade as 0.6423 above 0.9388, and no grouping of 0.9784, 0.9388 and 0.9132 gives either number, the mean of all three being 0.9435. Two different target series are used in one section for the same quantity, twenty years of SST for the correlation and forty-one years from 1980 for the grey model, and the relational coefficient is written as a function of k on the left and of t on the right. The forecast has no bound: a grey model with a negative development coefficient grows without limit, and the paper extrapolates to 2070 from a sequence whose own validation point already overshoots by 1.4 degrees. No density figure: 854 raw words on the span against 985 claimed, an overcount of thirteen percent.

note: Fortieth type-A record, the eighth instruction-template naming in a row, and the first of the eight whose stored count nearly matches the chapter: twelve moves crossed with three forms, thirty-six stored names for thirty-five located blocks, one block per move at the prose level with the third form of each move never separately realised. Only the move names anything: space-time separation interface, mean-removal matrix, snapshot covariance, ordered spatial-mode, coefficient extraction, energy-truncated field, trend-plus-periodicity, forecast coefficient-to-field, temperature-band location, first-order indicator accumulation, temperature-to-rate, threshold inversion. Span is the artifact's chapter, file pages 5 to 13: 3.1 the POD prediction of sea surface temperature through the snapshot definition, the covariance eigen-decomposition, the eigenvalue table and the three-mode truncation, the training and testing split, the error table, the assumption that modes are fixed for fifty years, and the trend-plus-Fourier forecast, then 3.2's thermal bands and months, then 4.1 the nutrient loss model from the first-order accumulation law through Arrhenius, the regressions, the parameter table, the storage-time formulas and the minimum rule, ending on the standards and the temperature table. Correct and checked, and this is the strongest arithmetic of the pass so far: the eigenvalue shares in Table 2 are consistent with each other, 4,645.04 over 0.9396 putting the total at 4,943.6 and every other row dividing into that total to its printed two decimals, and the first three then summing to 97.36 percent as claimed; the grid count is right, seventeen latitudes and forty longitudes spanning 16 and 39 degrees at one-degree steps; the two frequency factors are the exponentials of the printed intercepts, 1.495e10 and 3.951e19; the two activation energies are the printed slopes times the gas constant, 58,516.8 and 109,775.0 against 58,501.84 and 109,748.6 printed, a third of a percent out; and all ten cells of the storage-time table reproduce equations (7) and (8) to two decimals, the 6.03, 3.88, 2.54, 1.68, 1.13 column and the 15.11, 6.61, 2.97, 1.37, 0.65 column both. The minimum rule is also applied correctly, the two columns crossing between 290 and 295 kelvin. Verified defects. The snapshot count is wrong: the paper says m = 468, its own split is 446 training plus 12 testing, which is 458, and its own date range, December 1981 to January 2020 monthly, is 458 months, and the validation dates confirm 458, since snapshot 447 lands on February 2019 only if the first snapshot is December 1981, so 468 contradicts three other statements and the covariance's m minus one denominator is wrong by ten. The validation is a one-year holdout averaged into a fifty-year extrapolation: Table 3 prints four of the twelve test snapshots, and those four average 14.105 percent where the text claims 13.69, so the printed average cannot be checked from the printed rows, and a 13.7 percent error on the indicator they then use to locate fish is never compared with the size of the shift being predicted. The mode truncation keeps 97 percent of the variance and discards 3 percent without ever computing a reconstruction error, so what the truncation throws away is never carried into the forecast error. The trend-plus-periodicity forecast is stated in one sentence with no statement of how the two fittings combine, no window, no order, and no fit statistic. note: Part 1 of the paper, printed 3 to 10: the schedule problem is split into three cases by how disjoint the campsite sets are, then 5.2.1 partitions the campsites by residue modulo 25, one orbit per trip type, computes the distance a trip covers in a day and the number Q of intervals that buys, and builds the schedule from a leader that always travels at that rate with Q further trips launching behind it each day, the queue lengths z_i fixed by three constraints; then 5.2.2 replaces the 25 single-type orbits by 13 same-propulsion pairs for Y below the threshold, gives the two-day cycle for Y = 150 as a printed table of campsite sequences, and reads a capacity of 2,340 trips a year off it; then 5.2.3 generalises to orbits holding m types and stops. Seventeen text blocks over about 1,383 words, against a layout claim of 26 paragraphs and 2,070 words for printed 3 to 12, and this paper's pages separate paragraphs badly, so the block count is the seventeen blocks the page text preserves rather than the number of prose paragraphs. Seventeen blocks coded: five derive, four compute, two define, two select, one each of route, handoff, interpret and limit, and no source, read-figure, compare or check at all - the part cites nothing, compares its three cases nowhere, reads none of its six charts, and never checks a number against another. Defects: the eight-hour rule says a type is possible if A_i <= 8, type 1 fails at 225/(4 x 6) = 9.38 and is dropped, type 3 fails at 225/(4 x 7) = 8.03 and is kept because it is 'really close to 8' - and the whole construction then depends on the count being 25, since 5.2.1 partitions campsites by remainder modulo 25 and assigns one orbit per type, so a paper that had applied its own test would have had 24 types and a modulo-24 partition. The threshold that closes 5.2.1 is asserted rather than derived: Y >= 7 + ... + 18 + 6 + 7 + ... + 18 = 306 sums the durations of the 26 types, while the requirement actually used in the construction is a seven-campsite skeleton per type, which needs Y >= 175 and leaves 131 values of Y where the paper abandons a method that still works. And Q = [32Y/(25 x 225)] is below one for every Y under 176, so at the paper's own illustration value the leader construction launches zero trips a day and 5.2.1 produces no schedule at Y = 150 at all. And the capacity of 2,340 is 26 types times its own 90 two-day cycles, which is what the formula says but not what the schedule does: the M-6 row of the printed two-day table carries the same five campsites on both dates, so the only six-day type in the schedule launches every day and the table implies 2,430 trips a year, ninety more than the number quoted two lines below it. Stored field: 137 units over the eight pages, 13 distinct directive strings and 6 distinct excerpts, spread over four layout chapters - assumptions, model-establishment, model-improvement and algorithm - with printed 3 carrying 41 of the 137 and the remaining seven pages between 9 and 22 each.

function_strings: Vary one declared input family, retain the exact table, and qualify the managerial claim by the observed pattern. | Forecast the whole study by naming the decision, mechanism, case, outputs, and robustness variables. | Use familiar scheduling systems to motivate the shared resource-allocation structure before specializing to a river. | Define an operational state immediately before the algorithm consumes it. | State a simplification and explain the computational mechanism it enables. | Convert the current river state into a set of groups eligible for one campsite. | Give a normalized schedule score and interpret values above, below, and equal to one. | State the default daily rule, then add waitlist, ahead-of-schedule, and exit cases with explicit precedence. | Walk through a small assignment before presenting the complete repeated procedure. | Use a multi-day trace to expose long-run scheduling behavior and define the reported seasonal output. | Name a simplifying omission, explain its directional effect, and state what evidence is needed before transfer. | Translate a result into an action only after restating the ratio direction, operating conditions, and uncertainty boundary.
note: Section 2, Methods, on printed 6 to 9: four working definitions - an open campsite, moving to one, the waitlist and the exit - then the array representation of the river and the candidate set of the day, G_c = {g_i : m_i + l_i >= c}, then the four caveats that make that set operational, then the priority rule that picks which candidate takes the campsite, then the three caveats that constrain the choice, then a fourth figure that depicts the algorithm. Seventeen text blocks over about 877 words, against a layout claim of 33 paragraphs and 2,320 words for the same four pages over two layout chapters (model-establishment 6 to 8, algorithm 6 to 9). Nine blocks coded: three define, two handoff, one each of route, mechanism, derive and check, and no source, read-figure, compute, compare, select or interpret at all - the chapter cites nothing, computes nothing, compares nothing, and the four figures it prints are captions that narrate the algorithm rather than charts that are read. What this chapter is instead is a procedure written out in prose and then illustrated: the only relation in it is the priority ratio P = l_i t_i / (225 d_i), inherited from the variable list on printed 5 and never derived here, and the only argument is the mechanism block's, that moving the group furthest behind schedule first is what keeps every group on the river for exactly its trip length. The chapter's weakness is that its definitions are stated for a single campsite per step and its correctness is asserted rather than shown: nothing in the four pages proves that the daily sweep from the furthest empty campsite upstream terminates in a schedule, that the priority order is greedy-optimal, or that the three caveats cannot leave a group unable to reach the exit by its last night - the exit rule only forbids leaving early, it does not prevent arriving late. Stored field: 99 units over the four pages, 12 distinct directive strings and 4 distinct excerpts, spread over four layout chapters, with printed 7 carrying 37 of the 99 and printed 9, which is one figure and nothing else, carrying 9.

function_strings: State a modeling assumption, explain why it is plausible, and name the mathematical simplification it enables. | Forecast the decision, assumptions, model families, model-specific actions, and cross-model result before details. | Offer operational options and compare safety, autonomy, crowding, maintenance, and throughput. | Translate rising demand and one-resource-per-group occupancy into a capacity question. | Define every symbol immediately before the model or figure consumes it. | Build a restrictive analytic baseline and use it as a reference rather than a universal optimum. | Narrate an algorithm as ordered state transitions with triggers and failure recording. | Connect an adjustable parameter to a physical mechanism and then to a plotted trend. | Read a figure into an explicit threshold while retaining axes, scenario, uncertainty, and comparator. | Explain priority, feasible-site search, nearest-goal placement, removal, and itinerary output. | Move from process assumptions through conditioning and event decomposition to a decision probability. | Compare models by the assumptions managers can accept and the risks each leaves. | Pair a restrictive assumption with a specific extension that changes the mechanism.
note: Section 5.1, Base Case, on printed 6 to 8 (file pages 8 to 10): the tail of the Model 3 assumptions carried in from section 4.5, then the Approach pointer, then the four parameters S_i, E, v and D, then the three rescalings S' = S/24, v' = 24v/225 and D' = D/225, then the single equation of the chapter, dX = floor((E' - S')v'/D'), then the argument that the first n campsites can be filled and the fleet moved as a unit each day, then the send-off times s_i = E' - i D'/v', then the four partial derivatives of n with respect to E, S, v and D and the note that the D derivative is inverse square. Fourteen preserved text blocks over about 867 words, against a layout claim of 12 paragraphs and 1,020 words for the same three pages. Coded: seven define, three derive, two route and two mechanism, with source, select, compute, read-figure, compare, check, limit, interpret and handoff all absent. That shape is the point of the chapter: it is a closed-form baseline whose every element is a definition or a derivative, and the one place words are spent on interpretation, the sensitivity paragraph at the foot of printed 8, is carried inside the block that derives the derivatives rather than given a block of its own. There is no table, no figure, no worked season and no number beyond the conversion examples (16.5 for half past four, D' = 1/45 for five-mile spacing). What the chapter does have is the sentence that carries the whole of its authority, 'This is clearly the optimal way to use campsites, though the assumptions are quite restrictive', which is the optimality claim the rest of the paper leans on and which nothing in the three pages proves - the filling argument shows that a scheme exists which uses every campsite every night, not that no other scheme serves more boats, and the floor in equation (5) is never reconciled with the requirement that a boat's last night fall on the last campsite. Stored field: 37 units over the three pages, 13 distinct directive strings and 2 distinct source excerpts, distributed 19 on printed 6, 17 on printed 7 and 1 on printed 8, and the strings arrive in the same thirteen-item order on both of the full pages - the clearest case in the sample of a stored field that cycles its own taxonomy instead of following the prose.

function_strings: Derive a scheduling priority from remaining slack and mobility rather than presenting it as an arbitrary sort key. | Forecast the decision, assumptions, algorithm, evaluation metric, main result, sensitivity, and limitation before details. | Translate a technical threshold into an explicit operating input and action for a manager. | Separate throughput, contact, and schedule-repair objectives before selecting the main optimization focus. | Pair each simplification with its practical rationale and the algorithmic structure it enables. | Define object state and array axes before narrating transitions. | Show a complete code block and then explain it by line range and state effect. | Partition a scheduling step into completion, direct placement, fallback, and displacement cases. | Introduce one tunable constant, describe its mechanism, and report both throughput and repair effects. | Explain an abrupt simulation change through the floor-function reachability boundary that caused it. | Normalize completed trips by a campsite-night reference so larger seasons or site counts are comparable. | Vary one parameter, report direction and magnitude, identify threshold behavior, and state the operating implication. | Record the reusable contribution first and only then delimit its evidence and failure modes. | Turn model findings into short operational rules while retaining the assumptions that make them valid. | Trace an implementation from input generation through scheduling and printed diagnostics. | Separate contextual citation from empirical calibration and computational reproducibility.
note: Section 4, The Model, on printed 2 to 8 (file pages 4 to 10), read with the 204 Java source lines removed: twenty-one prose blocks over about 2,878 words, against a stored field that puts model-establishment on page 5 alone (40 of its 209 units, all on the page the listing starts) and algorithm across pages 6 to 9 (88 units) - so the layout's model chapter is the code listing and the prose model chapter is not. Coded: seven handoff, three define, two each of route, derive, mechanism and limit, and one each of source, check and compare, with select, compute, read-figure and interpret absent. This is the type's handoff-heavy chapter, a third of its blocks pointing at code: define the two components (a boat is a trip, the river is Y + 1 equally spaced sites), define the schedule as a table of sites by nights, announce the algorithm, then narrate the listing case by case - best case, nearly best case, third case, worst case with its role swap - each block carrying its line ranges. The two places the chapter does work of its own are worth separating from the narration. The mechanism is the role-swap argument, and it is a real proof sketch: a boat cannot move upstream, so the higher-priority boat must find another site, and the process terminates because 'no new boats have entered the river and at least one boat must have advanced a site to cause this problem, leaving an open site behind them'. The derive is the movement rule S_k = ceil((Y - S_k)/d_k), bounded by v_k h(225/(Y+1)) sites a day and then patched with a constant m_C, which is deferred to the results chapter. What the chapter never does is measure itself: there is no run, no count of trips, no check that the priority order it hypothesised on printed 2 actually reduces rescheduling, and the only check block is the exit scan that finds boats which cannot finish by the season's end. Its two figures are captions for case four rather than charts, so read-figure is absent in a chapter that prints two figures. Stored field: 209 units over the seven pages, 16 distinct directive strings and 5 distinct source excerpts, distributed 38, 40, 23, 22, 22, 62 and 2, with the 62 on printed 7 - the page that holds two equations and two short paragraphs - the largest single page in the span.

function_strings: Translate technical outputs into manager-facing capacity, schedule, model-choice, and implementation actions while preserving uncertainty. | Forecast the competing objectives, model mechanisms, quantitative tradeoffs, robustness, and conditional recommendation before details. | Introduce each new model as a response to a named failure or limitation of the previous construction. | Define schedule orientations, metrics, domains, and objectives before using them in algorithms or results. | Pair each simplification with empirical motivation and the scheduling behavior it enables or excludes. | Use a deliberately simple model to expose blocking and crossover mechanisms, then hand those failures to the next model. | State inputs and outputs, then narrate an ordered loop with branch conditions and state updates. | Justify urgency with remaining-distance slack and resolve collisions with feasibility and crossover-aware ranking. | Relax discrete campsite assignment into continuous positions, apply local repulsion, and map back only after separation. | Motivate structural heuristics, build a candidate sequence, test feasibility, saturate it, and spread the accepted schedule. | Declare ordered evaluation criteria, provide a scenario table, and interpret model-specific trends without hiding the comparator. | Compare models on throughput, crossover, distribution match, sensitivity, and management preference rather than one scalar alone. | Retain each reusable strength before naming its mechanism-specific weakness and concrete improvement path. | Convert findings into a conditional recommendation keyed to the decision maker's tolerance for crossover and occupancy loss. | Explain what a histogram, state diagram, schedule plot, or comparison chart makes inspectable and which claim it cannot prove alone. | Separate contextual references and borrowed river data from reproducible model inputs, code, and experiment outputs.
note: Section 4.1, the naive model, on printed 5 to 6 (file pages 6 and 7): the Models preamble, which defines optimal as no two trips at one campsite on one night and then argues that scheduling theory and queueing theory do not apply, then the naive model announced as a first exploration, then three insertion rules, then a pseudocode listing in five preserved fragments, then the listing's failure branch, then three stated problems and the handoff to the priority model. Fifteen preserved text blocks over about 450 words, five of them fragments of a single listing that the extractor split one instruction per block, so the block count here measures the listing rather than the argument. Coded: seven handoff, three define, three limit, one compare and one route, with derive, compute, read-figure, check, select, mechanism, interpret and source absent. The distribution is the furthest this type goes from paper 95 in the same problem: there is not one derivation in the chapter, no equation at all, and the only quantity named is the ratio distance remaining over days remaining, which is introduced here and used as a priority in the next model without a line of justification. The compare block is the paper's best single move and worth recording: it maps the problem onto scheduling n activities that each need Y+1 ordered jobs on Y+1 distinct machines, then says why the standard answers fail - parallel machines are identical, a sequence of jobs needs ordered precedence, and queueing theory assumes a queue can hold more than one, whereas here one occupant per site per night makes every arrival beyond the first balk with probability one. That is a real reduction with a real reason, and it is the only place in the chapter where the model choice is argued rather than asserted. What the chapter does not do is test the naive model at all: it is excluded from formal testing in one sentence, so the three stated problems are predictions, not findings, and the reader is asked to accept that crossovers and long trips blocking short ones are the failure modes without a single scheduled season shown. Stored field: 87 units over the two pages, 16 distinct directive strings and 3 distinct source excerpts, distributed 60 and 27, and the layout labels both pages algorithm rather than model-establishment - it puts the model on printed 8 to 10, where the density perturbation and bone growth models are, so the layout takes the third model for the model chapter and skips the first.
